papers.title: Interaction-Induced Topological Transport of Extended Doublons
papers.summary: Topological boundary states are a defining feature of topological systems, providing robust transport protected against perturbations. While such states are commonly engineered in non-interacting systems, how to realize interaction-induced topological states composed of only few particles has remained experimentally unexplored thus far. In this work, we realize such states using a driven photonic lattice as a linear analogue platform. We observe the formation of spatially extended bound states of two interacting particles, in which the particles remain correlated while occupying different lattice sites. At discrete values of the local interaction, these bound states support robust transport governed by a topological phase arising from drive-induced correlated hopping. Our results establish an experimentally accessible route to interaction-driven topology beyond single-particle physics and provide a versatile framework for exploring correlated few-particle phenomena across different physical platforms.

papers.title: Landscape of scattering universality with general dispersion relations
papers.summary: Universality in physics describes how disparate systems can exhibit identical low-energy behavior. Here, we reveal a rich landscape of new universal scattering phenomena governed by the interplay between an interaction and a system's density of states. We investigate one-dimensional scattering with dispersion relations $\epsilon(k)=|k|^m$ and $\epsilon(k)=\operatorname{sgn}(k)|k|^m$ for any real $m>1$. For emitter scattering and separable potentials, including contact potentials, we classify the zero-energy $S$-matrix limits. These universal $S$-matrix fixed points depend solely on the dispersion exponent $m$ and a finite set of integers characterizing the low-momentum interaction structure. This classification extends far beyond the standard quadratic-dispersion case ($m=2$). We further derive a generalized Levinson's theorem relating the total winding of the $S$-matrix determinant to the number of bound states. Finally, for contact potentials and analytic monomial dispersions, we analyze the leading low-energy expansion of the scattering phase near these fixed points and extract the corresponding Wigner-delay scaling. Our findings are directly relevant to synthetic quantum systems, where engineered dispersion relations in atomic arrays and photonic crystals offer a platform to explore these universal behaviors.

papers.title: Reservoir computing based predictive reduced order model for steel grade intermixing in an industrial continuous casting tundish
papers.summary: Continuous casting is a widely adopted process in the steel industry, where maintaining high steel quality is paramount. Efficient prediction of grade intermixing during ladle changeover operations is critical for maintaining steel quality and minimizing material losses in the continuous casting process. Among various factors influencing grade intermixing, operating parameters play a significant role, in addition to tundish geometry and flow control devices. In this study, three-dimensional, transient, two-phase turbulent flow simulations are conducted to investigate the ladle changeover operation. During this process, the molten steel level in the tundish typically varies over time, significantly affecting the grade intermixing phenomena. The influence of ladle change time on intermixing time has been presented. However, high-fidelity full-order simulations of such complex transient phenomena are computationally expensive and are impractical for real-time monitoring or design-space exploration in industrial-scale applications. To address this issue, a reduced order modelling approach based on proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and reservoir computing (RC) is employed to efficiently predict intermixing time. The proposed reduced order model (ROM) demonstrates excellent predictive accuracy using limited training data while requiring significantly less computational resources and training time. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed methodology as a fast, reliable tool for real-time process monitoring and optimization in industrial continuous casting operations.

papers.title: Thermodynamic selection of stationary Rayleigh-B\'enard flow states with slip and no-slip boundaries
papers.summary: Multiple stationary flow states may exist under the same external/boundary conditions, while the hydrodynamic equations alone do not provide a global criterion for determining which of these states is preferentially selected. Here, we formulate and test such a criterion for stationary Rayleigh-B\'enard (RB) convection within a global non-equilibrium thermodynamic description (Ho\l yst et al., EPL 149, 30001 (2025)). We find that each stationary flow state in RB convection is characterized by the state function $\mathcal{F}=-E_k-\Psi$, where $E_k$ is the macroscopic kinetic energy of the flow and $\Psi$ is a thermodynamic state function that emerges from the nonlinear inertial term in the Navier-Stokes equation and is associated with the compression and redistribution of the gas accompanying the formation of the convective state. Changes in $\mathcal{F}$ correspond to path-independent work between stationary states. We show that, among dynamically accessible stationary states, the state with the lower value of $\mathcal{F}$ is more stable and is preferentially selected. Both the macroscopic kinetic energy acquired by the flow and the accompanying thermodynamic reorganization of the gas therefore contribute in the same direction to lowering $\mathcal{F}$ and stabilizing the stationary state. We test the criterion using numerical solutions of the hydrodynamic equations for Rayleigh-B\'enard convection with both slip and no-slip boundary conditions. For both types of boundary, the observed selection of competing stationary states is consistent with the thermodynamic prediction. The resulting state function provides a global criterion for the selection and stability of stationary hydrodynamic states. It establishes a direct connection between the nonlinear dynamics of the Navier-Stokes equation, thermodynamic work, and macroscopic flow stability.

papers.title: Role of interchange and mixed modes in magnetic Rayleigh-Taylor instability dynamics --- a 2D vs 3D study
papers.summary: The magnetic Rayleigh-Taylor instability (MRTI) governs plasma mixing and transport in diverse systems. Owing to computational constraints, two-dimensional (2D) MRTI simulations are common. It is intuitive that 2D and three-dimensional (3D) counterparts differ significantly. One of the crucial differences is the types of wave modes admissible in the two systems. Perturbations in 3D MRTI facilitate the coexistence of interchange, undular, and mixed modes. Such rich physics is not possible in 2D, where the perturbations can only have undular modes. This raises the question, how do the interchange and mixed modes change the MRTI dynamics? To address this aspect, we simulate MRTI in 2D and 3D, across different magnetic field strengths. Consequently, this paper provides, currently lacking, a rigorous qualitative and quantitative evaluation of the similarities and differences between 2D and 3D MRTI. The 2D MRTI is characterized by large-scale plumes with inefficient mixing and significant fluid interpenetration, while the 3D is characterized by significant mixing and small-scale plumes. Consequently, higher gravitational potential energy is extracted in 2D. The small-scale vortices and large current sheets lead to higher energy dissipation in 3D. Extending to fundamental nature of evolution, 3D simulations tend towards a self-similar state (due to interchange and mixed modes). But such behaviour was not observed in our 2D simulations, due to the persistent influence of magnetic field. Surprisingly, the reconnection driven magnetic-to-kinetic energy conversion is similar in 2D and 3D. Overall, the work concludes that interchange and mixed modes influence the dynamics significantly leading to stark differences between 2D and 3D MRTI. The work thus guides the extent to which one can extrapolate the 2D simulations results to understand MRTI in astrophysical and fusion energy systems.

papers.title: Voltage-Dependent Photocurrent and Crossover Behavior in Crystalline Silicon Solar Cells
papers.summary: Contrary to the conventional assumption of voltage-independent photocurrent, we show that the photocurrent in monocrystalline silicon p-n junction solar cells depends explicitly on voltage. By applying physically realistic boundary conditions to the classical p-n junction solar-cell model, we derive an analytical expression for the photocurrent that incorporates both the built-in potential and the applied voltage. The model predicts a crossover point between the dark and illuminated $I-V$ characteristics, irrespective of illumination intensity. This prediction is experimentally validated by lock-in measurements on a commercial monocrystalline silicon solar cell. These results establish a more consistent understanding of the quantitative role of the built-in potential in the photovoltaic effect.

papers.title: From First Principles to Multi-scale Decomposition: Mutual Information as a Segregation Index
papers.summary: Segregation operates across demographic and spatial scales and requires careful and principled measurement. In this work, we derive mutual information from well-known general approaches to constructing segregation indices and interpret the mathematical properties that are unique to it. The properties relate mainly to its behaviour when demographic identities and spatial units are coarse-grained. Mutual information decomposes into the contributions of regions and supergroups, which reveals insights that would be inaccessible otherwise. We demonstrate this with an exploratory case study of residential ethnic segregation in England and Wales. Overall, we help researchers identify when mutual information is the only suitable segregation index and provide open source software to support multi-scale analysis.

papers.title: An Information-Thermodynamic Accounting Framework for Planetary Biosphere Productivity
papers.summary: Planetary primary producers use stellar or internally generated free energy to maintain biomass and produce new material. We formulate the associated productivity ceiling while separating environmental losses, basal maintenance, retained biomass energy and net dissipation from heritable copying. Maintenance copy-reset cycles and copies retained in new biomass have distinct thermodynamic costs. For a specified feasible producer population, the normalized ceiling is $(1-x_0)/(1+q)$, where $x_0$ is the baseline copying fraction and $q$ is the growth-associated copying cost relative to other production costs. Exact interval bounds and global sensitivity analyses quantify both effects without assigning empirical probabilities to unmeasured biological parameters. Observation-constrained planetary resources and strain-matched genome and cellular-carbon measurements provide separate physical and biological benchmarks. For the two mean inventories, a 10\% growth-copying correction requires an effective copying cost $e_g\chi$ about 63--84 times a published DNA fuel benchmark at unit production efficiency; the benchmark is not a measured dissipation cost. We also show that partitioning an already measured total maintenance budget cannot change the absolute productivity ceiling, and that population adjustment can preserve information-load fractions as supply falls. The framework provides conditional feasibility tests, inverse thresholds and measurement priorities, rather than a calibrated prediction of extraterrestrial productivity.

papers.title: Maximum Velocity of a Liquid Metal Drop Driven by a Time-Dependent Electrocapillary Excitation
papers.summary: Gallium alloys are promising materials in biomedical engineering, electronics, and wireless communications, thanks to their good conductivity, non toxicity and their ability to sustain large deformations. They can be transported in capillaries using purely electric means by continuous electrowetting (CEW). Current models of CEW-driven flows do not address the transient response to fast changes in the excitation, crucial in many applications. Here, we present a theory that describes the CEW-driven oscillatory motion of a drop of Eutectic Gallium-Indium alloy inside a capillary. We consider inertia, viscosity and the transient response of the electrical circuit consisting of the drop plus the electrolyte where it is immersed. The theory describes fairly well the experimental drop velocity and explains the existence of an optimal frequency that maximizes the velocity.

papers.title: Data-driven reduced order model for residence time distribution analysis of an industrial-scale continuous casting tundish
papers.summary: The continuous casting tundish plays a critical role as a metallurgical reactor in the continuous casting process, with its flow characteristics serving as a key parameter in the production of high-quality steel. These characteristics are typically assessed through residence time distribution (RTD) curves. This study examines the flow behaviour in a single-strand continuous casting tundish through a combination of numerical simulations and experimental validation. Steady-state full order model (FOM) simulations are performed under both isothermal and non-isothermal conditions to evaluate the influence of thermal buoyancy on the velocity field, which is found to be negligible. The resulting flow fields are used to initialize transient tracer transport simulations for determining the RTD and flow volume partitioning. Subsequently, a data-driven reduced order model (ROM) is developed to predict the RTD response. Comparison of RTD curves obtained from experiments, FOM, and ROM shows excellent agreement, with the ROM accurately capturing the key flow characteristics at a fraction of the computational cost. These results highlight the potential of ROM techniques for efficient real-time analysis, design, and optimization of tundish operations in metallurgical processes.

papers.title: Ultra-broadband Mid to Long-wave Infrared Spintronic Poisson Bolometer
papers.summary: Infrared detectors have traditionally been divided into two fundamental classes, mid-wave (MWIR, 3-5 um) and long-wave (LWIR, 8-14 um). Integrating MWIR and LWIR within a single device is challenging due to distinct materials, cooling needs, and detection mechanisms, while such integration is critical for improved object recognition, temperature estimation, and environmental sensing. In this work, we demonstrate a Spintronic Poisson (SP) bolometer enabling room-temperature ultra-broadband sensing across 3-14 um. Unlike conventional bolometers that rely on continuous analog signals, the SP bolometer implements a Poisson-counting detection paradigm, encoding temperature in discrete stochastic events, which turns thermal noise from a limitation into the basis of the estimator itself. We fabricate the SP bolometer using a spintronic transduction layer integrated with a plasmonic nanoantenna array to enhance broadband infrared absorption. Using spintronic transduction, the device achieves the noise-equivalent temperature difference (NETD, thermal sensitivity metric) of 80-100 mK at 300 K, surpassing uncooled detectors and approaching cooled technologies. This work establishes a statistical detection paradigm for room-temperature infrared sensing with broad application potential.

papers.title: Diffusion Model Driven Airfoil Design: From Geometry Encoding to Practical Applications
papers.summary: The diffusion model, the state-of-the-art generative machine-learning architecture, has shown promising results in airfoil inverse designs. In this study, we implement and trained a series of diffusion models on three different airfoil geometry data encoding formats -- principal component weights, ordered $x$-$y$ coordinates, and 2D signed distance functions (SDF) -- to generate 2D airfoils. By systematically comparing the performance of diffusion models trained on different data structures, it is found that for 2D airfoil design problems, the diffusion model performs the best when directly trained with coordinates. Training with latent space (principal component weights in this study) limits the model's design freedom and decreases the training effectiveness. Although the 2D SDF data appear to result in the least performing model, it proves its feasibility in aerodynamic shape generation, paving the way toward 3D problems where SDF is more favored. This study also investigated deploying the diffusion model in practical engineering applications. A multi-target optimization procedure is proposed based on the stochastic nature of the diffusion process, which drastically simplifies the procedure compared to conventional methods. The extrapolation performance of the model is also investigated by tasking the model with both aerodynamic and flow condition labels that are extrapolated beyond the training set boundaries.

papers.title: Angle-Dependent Dose Transformer Algorithm for Fast Proton Therapy Dose Calculations
papers.summary: Monte Carlo (MC) dose engines are the gold standard for pencil beam scanning proton therapy, but their computational cost limits adaptive workflows and other tasks requiring repeated dose recalculation. Existing deep learning beamlet dose engines require each beamlet to be sampled in its beam's-eye-view, which implies a local resampling of the computed tomography (CT) patch for every beamlet. We propose the Angle-dependent Dose Transformer Algorithm (ADoTA), which adds an input channel encoding a fast analytical beamlet shape projection that supplies the beam direction explicitly. The CT is resampled only once per irradiation field to an isotropic $2\times2\times2$ mm$^3$ grid, and each beamlet is obtained by cropping this shared grid. The model was trained on CT data from 108 patients for initial energies of 70 to 150 MeV (thoracic) and 70 to 270 MeV (abdominal/pelvic) and evaluated on an independent test cohort of 50 patients. ADoTA achieved $\Gamma(1\%,3\,\mathrm{mm},0.1\%)$ pass rates of $99.40\pm0.86\%$ (thoracic) and $99.87\pm0.23\%$ (abdominal/pelvic), with an effective batched throughput of $3.14\pm0.31$ ms per beamlet. In a 5640-spot prostate plan benchmark with both routes optimized on the GPU, the analytical projection reduced the plan's direction-encoding cost by $9.6\times$ and its total compute time by $1.48\times$ compared with local beam's-eye-view sampling. For full treatment plans, $\Gamma(2\%,2\,\mathrm{mm},10\%)$ pass rates averaged 95.1% (lung) and 96.1% (prostate), while the target $D_{98\%}$ was underestimated by 1.8 to 2.5% of prescription in prostate plans and 4.2 to 5.9% in thoracic plans. ADoTA achieves close to MC accuracy at the beamlet level without beamlet-specific resampling, with a clinically relevant target underdosage in thoracic plans that should be resolved before clinical use.

papers.title: Automated Detection and Climatological Analysis of Ripple-Scale Gravity Wave Instabilities Using a Squeeze-and-Excitation Convolutional Neural Network
papers.summary: All-sky OH airglow imaging provides two-dimensional observations of mesospheric wave morphology near the nominal OH emission peak altitude. Small, localized ripple-like structures are difficult to catalogue consistently through manual inspection and may represent either instability-related features or secondary gravity waves. We present an automated detection framework based on a squeeze-and-excitation convolutional neural network (SE-CNN) trained on 41 x 41-pixel patches extracted from 512 x 512-pixel all-sky images acquired at Yucca Ridge Field Station. Signed differences between consecutive images separated by approximately 2 min are normalized using spatial median-absolute-deviation scaling before classification. The trained model is applied to complete images through sliding-window inference, followed by score-map reconstruction, component filtering, and spatial matching. On the held-out patch test set, the classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.92, precision of 0.89, recall of 0.93, and F1 score of 0.92. Within a selected cohort of manually positive validation frames, 299 of 415 evaluable frames contained at least one reference-automated spatial overlap, and 324 of 559 eligible reference supports received a one-to-one automated-component assignment. In a separate blinded single-reviewer audit of disagreement patches, 411 of 543 model-candidate/reference-unmarked crops were classified as clear ripple-like, corresponding to a clear-ripple fraction of 75.7% with a night-cluster bootstrap 95% interval of 70.4%-80.2%. Because the audit was restricted to selected disagreement cases from manually positive frames, this value is not an archive-wide precision estimate.

papers.title: Weak Singularity of Navier-Stokes Equations Based on Energy Estimation in Sobolev Space
papers.summary: Based on Dou Huashu's energy gradient theory, this paper focuses on the weak singularity of the incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations in steady, fully developed flows. When the gradient of total mechanical energy is perpendicular to the streamline (i.e., $ u_j \frac{\partial E}{\partial x_j} = 0 $), substituting this critical condition into the NS equations with no-slip boundary conditions leads to the viscous term $ \nu \to 0 $. To rigorously analyze the regularity of the solution, Sobolev space $ H_0^1(\Omega) $ is introduced for energy estimation. The results show that the velocity field loses $ H^1 $-regularity, and the NS equations degenerate into Euler equations, which admit discontinuous weak solutions. Thus, the position where the mechanical energy gradient is perpendicular to the streamline becomes a weak singularity of the NS equations.

papers.title: A Stable, High-Order Time-Stepping Scheme for the Drift-Diffusion Model in Modern Solar Cell Simulation
papers.summary: This paper presents a one-dimensional transient drift-diffusion simulator for advanced solar cells, integrating a structure-preserving finite-volume spatial discretization with Scharfetter-Gummel-type fluxes and a high-order, L-stable implicit Runge-Kutta (Radau IIA) temporal integrator. The scheme ensures local charge conservation, handles sharp material interfaces, achieves second-order spatial and fifth-order temporal convergence, and exhibits excellent computational efficiency and numerical stability. Its accuracy is verified against the classical depletion approximation in p-n junction and validated against four independent software implementations for an organic photovoltaic device under a common protocol. The framework's extensibility is demonstrated by incorporating exciton kinetics in organic solar cells, capturing multi-timescale dynamics, and by modeling mobile ions in perovskite solar cells, reproducing characteristic J-V hysteresis without empirical parameters. This work provides a robust, high-order numerical foundation for simulating coupled charge, exciton, and ion transport in next-generation photovoltaic devices.

papers.title: Assessment of Latent Pedestrian-Vehicle Interaction Risk Profiles at Midblock Crossing in VR
papers.summary: Pedestrian safety at midblock crossings is a critical concern in mixed traffic environments where autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) share the road. Pedestrians often infer intent from vehicle motion in AV encounters, making them vulnerable to small shifts in conflict margins. This study investigates whether virtual reality (VR) crossing sessions separate into distinct interaction risk profiles and whether AV-only sessions shift profile prevalence compared to HDV-only sessions. Using large-scale immersive VR experiments from Toronto, Canada, and Newcastle, England, we compute surrogate safety measures (SSMs) and apply latent profile analysis (LPA) to identify distinct pedestrian crossing stances, ranging from risk-accepting to highly cautious. Key findings show that Newcastle exhibits a higher prevalence of high-urgency risk profiles in AV-only sessions, indicating that AVs contribute to higher-risk encounters. In contrast, Toronto shows no significant difference between AV-only and HDV-only sessions, suggesting that contextual factors influence the impact of AVs on pedestrian safety.

papers.title: Control of the bootstrap current in approximately quasi-axisymmetric magnetic fields
papers.summary: Quasi-axisymmetric stellarators are the stellarator analogue of axisymmetric tokamaks, retaining many of their favorable confinement properties, their compactness and their relative coil simplicity, while avoiding their principal limitation, the need for an inductively driven plasma current. Despite these attractive physics properties, the development of quasi-axisymmetric configurations has been severely constrained by the absence of an experimentally validated divertor concept compatible with their large bootstrap current. In this Letter, approximately quasi-axisymmetric fields, complemented with piecewise omnigenous perturbations, are proposed as the basis for a new strategy towards a stellarator reactor that potentially achieves, simultaneously, simple coil geometries, tokamak-like confinement and, through tailoring of the bootstrap current, compatibility with an island divertor. Implications for attaining a high bootstrap current fraction in tokamak devices are also discussed.

papers.title: Fluctuations in Aharonov-Bohm Electrodynamics
papers.summary: We consider the application of the Fluctuation Dissipation Theorem (FDT) to the electrodynamics of Aharonov-Bohm (ABE), which differs from Maxwell's in that it allows for local non-conservation of charge. For the case of a system of non-conserved charges at thermal equilibrium we obtain the same spectral distribution of energy of the electromagnetic field as in Maxwell electrodynamics. However, the electric field contribution to that energy doubles that in Maxwell case, while the magnetic contribution is the same as in Maxwell theory, the electric excess energy is compensated by a negative contribution arising form the Aharonov-Bohm (AB) scalar field. For a conductor with local non-conservation of charge described by the $\gamma$ model, we derive the spectrum of current correlation at first order in $\gamma$, which results in a violet noise contribution added to the classical Johnson-Nyquist white noise result for the voltage fluctuations in a conductor.

papers.title: Minimal seeds in the Stokes boundary layer
papers.summary: Minimal seeds are the smallest amplitude perturbations that trigger transition to turbulence in a subcritical flow. They are presented in the Stokes boundary layer, the oscillating flow of a viscous fluid above a flat plate, at a fixed initial phase corresponding to the timing of the Stokes boundary layer's optimal linear transient growth, at two moderate Reynolds numbers, and in two domains accommodating one and two wavelengths of the linearly optimal growing mode. Although the minimal seed trajectories are dominated by the flow's large linear transient growth at early times, only 77% of the initial energy is formed from the linearly optimal growing mode; the remainder ensures that nonlinear interaction transfers energy from spanwise- to streamwise- independent structures, and makes up for a timing mismatch between the end of linear transient growth and the production phase of the edge state (the saddle point separating the laminar and turbulent basins of attraction).

papers.title: Lacunarity in a Two-Dimensional Atomizing Liquid Jet
papers.summary: Atomization stretches and folds the liquid--gas interface before fragmenting it into ligaments and droplets, making fractal measures a natural descriptor of the lacunarity of the final breakup state. We examine this idea in two-dimensional (2D) VOF-DNS of a liquid jet with adaptive mesh refinement in Basilisk. Box-counting of the full resolved interface does not yield a single scale-independent exponent. Instead, two scaling ranges appear, separated by a crossover near the box-counting level \(L_{\mathrm{box}}\simeq7\): coarser boxes measure the folded connected jet envelope, whereas finer boxes increasingly sample ligaments, droplets, and nearly smooth local interface segments. Decomposing the interface into detached droplets, ligaments, and the connected main body shows that the relevant effective dimension is structure dependent. Droplets are most lacunar with dimension below one, ligaments occupy an intermediate level, and the main body carries the largest coarse-scale dimension. This hierarchy persists over $Re_l=100$--$10^4$ at fixed $\We_g=200$. The lacunarity of droplets is reminiscent of that of the object positions in the night sky hypothesized by de Vaucouleurs.

papers.title: Theory for the power threshold of the L-H transition in tokamaks
papers.summary: Flux-driven two-fluid simulations in a diverted tokamak exhibit a confinement transition when a critical heating threshold is exceeded, as in experimental observations of the L-H transition. The simulations show that electromagnetic drift-wave turbulence spontaneously generates a sheared $E\times B$ flow responsible for transport suppression in the edge. The toroidal-field asymmetry of the transition, here reproduced in simulations for the first time, arises from time-reversal symmetry breaking by finite collisionality, as demonstrated by a quasilinear calculation of the turbulent momentum flux. Scaling laws are analytically derived for the L-H power threshold in the high- and low-density branches, for the density minimum, and for the minimum power, all matching or surpassing the accuracy of existing empirical scalings.

papers.title: Quantifying thermal-signature equivalence in infrared breast thermography using a modified Pennes bioheat model
papers.summary: Infrared breast thermography measures skin-surface temperature, but heat diffusion and thermal screening can obscure intratumoral physiology. We introduce a tolerance-aware, full-profile framework to determine when distinct intratumoral perfusion patterns become observationally equivalent at the breast surface. We solve a steady-state modified Pennes model for a two-dimensional multilayer breast containing a finite tumor with uniform, rim-enhanced, necrotic-core, or anisotropic perfusion. A conservative finite-difference scheme with a BiCGSTAB solver and an incomplete-LU (IncompleteLUT) preconditioner is verified by mesh refinement and an analytical benchmark. For a representative configuration, equivalent-pair fractions are $2/6$, $5/6$, and $6/6$ at tolerances of $0.020$, $0.050$, and $0.100~^\circ\mathrm{C}$, respectively. Noise tests show that classification depends on how profile-level uncertainty is modeled. Matching tumor-averaged perfusion reduces rim-enhanced--uniform and necrotic-core--uniform profile distances by $97.7\%$ and $99.0\%$, respectively, whereas anisotropic perfusion remains more distinguishable. Greater tumor depth increases thermal-signature equivalence, while larger diameter enhances distinguishability. Among four parameter groups, heat generation has the strongest positive influence on mean profile separation. For fixed representative geometry and perfusion-pattern shapes, a 300-point Latin-hypercube analysis with independent uniform $\pm20\%$ perturbations of these parameter groups finds that about $79\%$ of sampled configurations retain at least one equivalent pair at $\varepsilon_T=0.020~^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Our results show that a detectable static surface anomaly does not uniquely determine its internal perfusion structure.

papers.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model for Radiotherapy Patient Scheduling under Realistic Clinical and Operational Constraints: a Feasibility Study
papers.summary: Radiotherapy scheduling must balance clinical constraints and operational objectives. We evaluated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate treatment schedules through simulation and retrospective clinical comparison. A one-year simulation modeled 1,400 new patients across 12 treatment categories and three linear accelerators (LINACs). Structured prompts provided ChatGPT with patient information, schedule status, clinical rules, and operational objectives. Scenarios assessed treatment-time consistency, LINAC continuity, gap reduction, and handling of infeasible requests. LLM schedules were compared with heuristic and constraint programming (CP-SAT) approaches under two objective settings. A six-week retrospective analysis included 2,043 clinical appointments. LLM-generated schedules met all predefined feasibility constraints in the evaluated scenarios, with 98.6-98.8% of fractions within preferred treatment-time windows. Prioritizing LINAC continuity reduced switching from 52.4 +/- 2.6% to 9.4 +/- 0.6%. Gap-constrained temporal relaxation reduced average daily gaps to 47.1 +/- 8.5 minutes and Friday gaps to 89.2 +/- 18.4 minutes while maintaining low overtime. The framework identified predefined violations in infeasible requests and suggested corrective actions. Heuristic and CP-SAT methods also generated feasible schedules, with performance dependent on objective weighting. In retrospective evaluation, all approaches scheduled appointments without overtime; LLM strategies reduced mean gaps by 50.8-77.1% and improved treatment-time consistency from 86.7% to 99.5-99.9%. These findings support further evaluation of structured LLM scheduling as a human-in-the-loop decision-support approach for radiotherapy.

papers.title: Colloquium: Nuclear clocks
papers.summary: The Th-229 nuclear isomeric state has the lowest energy of all known nuclear excited states, placing it within the reach of current table-top laser technology. This extraordinary property has made this nuclear isomer an attractive candidate for a nuclear optical clock of incredibly high precision and accuracy, both as isolated trapped Th-229 ions and embedded into solid-state platforms. Activity around Th-229 has surged in recent years, driven by breakthroughs in its direct laser excitation. The underlying nuclear physics that gives rise to this unique isomer will be elucidated, as well as the nearly half-century of efforts that led to its direct excitation. The design and systematics of a Th-229 nuclear clock will be discussed, both in ion traps and in the solid-state. These systematics, such as frequency shifts and quenching channels, can be leveraged both to probe the local chemical environment, and as a control knob during clock operation. Finally, the nuclear clock's high sensitivity to the variations of fundamental constants will be discussed.

papers.title: Feasibility of a Flexible, Hybrid Tokamak-Stellarator Experiment using an Axisymmetric Dipole Coil Array
papers.summary: We demonstrate the design of a flexible, university-scale hybrid tokamak-stellarator experiment based on an axisymmetric array of planar HTS dipole coils. Because the coil array has few geometric degrees of freedom, we use single-stage optimization of the coil currents initialized from two-stage solutions to obtain mutually consistent equilibria and coil sets within realistic engineering limits. We find that the field error and coil current thresholds set minimum and maximum coil-plasma distances that confine the boundary to a roughly fixed axisymmetric envelope, within which rotational transform, volume, coil current, and quasi-symmetry (QS) error trade off against one another. Tighter current limits delocalize the non-axisymmetric shaping and raise QS error at fixed transform. From this single coil array we obtain a broad range of equilibria-quasi-axisymmetric vacuum stellarators with $\iota$ up to 0.2, finite-$\beta$ hybrids with realistic profiles reaching on-axis $\iota$ $\approx$ 1 and vacuum transform relevant for MHD stabilization, and strongly shaped tokamaks with elongation $\kappa$ = 1.7 and triangularity $\delta$ = $\pm$0.6, all at peak pointwise coil forces well below the HTS tolerance. We show the same array can additionally correct toroidal field (TF) coil ripple, reducing the number of TF coils required compared to the equivalent tokamak. These results establish the design as a promising platform for hybrid tokamak-stellarator research.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for coupled stiff transport systems
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN) struggle with stiff, regime-changing transport equations due to instability, loss imbalance, and violations of physical consistency. This paper investigates these failures through the Marshak wave equations, a canonical benchmark from radiative transport, where initial and boundary conditions differ by up to 12 orders of magnitude, and proposes modifications to the standard PINN framework to overcome them. Three modifications are introduced: a ScaledSigmoid final activation enforcing physical bounds and positivity of the unknowns; a logarithmic MSE loss replacing the standard quadratic loss for initial and boundary conditions, enabling training across extreme scale disparities; and explicit enforcement of global conservation laws as an additional physics loss term. Monte Carlo sampling with exponential time weighting is used throughout. The proposed framework recovers the Marshak wave dynamics - including the hot, cold, and wave-front regions - in good agreement with a reference Implicit Monte Carlo solution (sub-millimeter absolute error on the front position, although the relative error remains substantial at early times), with run times under 5 minutes. Ablation studies confirm that each ingredient is essential: linear activation, absence of the logarithmic loss, or removal of the PDE term each independently cause the method to fail qualitatively. This work identifies and resolves three concrete failure modes of standard PINN on stiff hyperbolic systems with nonlinear coupling. The combination of bounded activations, scale-aware loss functions, and conservation law enforcement constitutes a framework validated on the present one-dimensional Marshak wave problem, with potential extension to other coupled stiff transport systems in engineering.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for shock capturing in inviscid flows around an airfoil
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown promise in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, shock capturing remains challenging for PINNs, particularly in steady flows around an airfoil, where shocks may not even be captured. In this study, we point out that the steady Euler equations used to construct the loss function impose weak constraints, which make it difficult to correct the continuous function approximation preference of neural networks, causing gradient descent to converge to a smooth local optimum. Based on this insight, we propose to strengthen the physical constraints by reconstructing steady shock capturing as a temporal evolution process governed by the unsteady Euler equations. The temporal evolution law of the flow field guides gradient descent, thereby alleviating its tendency to converge to smooth local optima and ensuring shock formation. We introduce a PDE loss function incorporating a pseudo-time stepping mechanism to obtain the steady state solution without solving the unsteady Euler equations over a long time interval. In addition, we develop a simplified formulation of the Euler equations to reduce the complexity of the PDE loss function, thereby improving shock capturing accuracy. By solving four forward problems involving different flow conditions and geometries, we verify that the proposed method achieves high accuracy in shock capturing while reducing the wall time to one-seventh of that required by existing advanced methods. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates its capability to solve a parametric problem involving the angle of attack and Mach number without relying on any labeled data.

papers.title: Full-data accuracy with fewer labels for training and fine-tuning machine-learning force fields
papers.summary: Machine-learning force fields (MLFFs) are reliable only near their training distribution, making efficient construction of diverse training sets a major bottleneck for both train-from-scratch and foundation fine-tuning workflows. Active learning can reduce this cost, but standard model-committee uncertainty is impractical for foundation MLFFs because each committee member requires a separate fine-tuning run. We present an active-learning workflow based on last-layer-projection regression (LLPR), a forward-pass-cheap per-configuration uncertainty estimator. Across molecular, condensed-phase, and electrolyte systems, LLPR identifies compact, high-value training sets that recover full-data accuracy using only a small fraction of electronic-structure labels. In foundation-model fine-tuning, LLPR-selected configurations approach the practical fine-tuning ceiling with substantially fewer labels than random selection. In iterative electrolyte fine-tuning, LLPR detects unphysical local coordination before new labelling, calibrates uncertainty in force-error units, and supports retrospective convergence monitoring. The resulting models reproduce reference density and Li--O coordination structure, providing a scalable uncertainty-quantification strategy across MLFF training regimes.

papers.title: Split Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Forward and Inverse Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
papers.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can solve forward and inverse PDE problems but may struggle with spectral bias and oscillatory, high-frequency, or phase-dependent solutions. We introduce a generalized split complex-valued PINN (SCV-PINN) framework with complex-valued parameters and latent representations. Split activations act separately on real and imaginary components while complex operations preserve their coupling, enabling amplitude--phase representations with practical optimization. Ablation studies evaluate split activation functions and collocation sampling strategies. Forward and inverse benchmarks include the Burgers, Allen--Cahn, Korteweg--de Vries, nonlinear Schr\"odinger, Helmholtz, and Poisson equations on regular and irregular domains; Kovasznay flow ($\mathrm{Re}=20$); lid-driven cavity flow ($\mathrm{Re}=100$); the Lorenz system; and inverse Burgers and Navier--Stokes problems ($\mathrm{Re}=100$). A three-dimensional Navier--Stokes Beltrami flow further demonstrates applicability to higher-dimensional nonlinear dynamics, with a relative $L_2$ error of $4.07\times10^{-5}$. Across these tests, SCV-PINN yields high-fidelity solutions and effective parameter identification, improving on real-valued PINNs and selected variants. The results suggest that split complex-valued representations can help address spectral-bias-related difficulties in nonlinear and oscillatory physical systems.

papers.title: Current-Sheet Formation in Electron Magnetohydrodynamics with Split Fractional Dissipation
papers.summary: Thin current sheets are central small-scale structures in electron magnetohydrodynamics (EMHD), closely associated with energy dissipation and fast magnetic reconnection at electron scales. We study their formation numerically in a $2\frac{1}{2}$-dimensional EMHD system on a periodic domain with split fractional dissipation, where the magnetic potential and the vertical magnetic component are damped separately. The local theory is governed by a symmetric combined damping balance, but the numerical onset of small-scale growth need not follow this symmetry. A scaling analysis identifies the out-of-plane current as the primary concentration observable, since it is regularized only through the magnetic-potential equation. Using a validated Fourier pseudospectral exponential time-differencing solver with resolution-controlled diagnostics, we find a clear decay/concentration dichotomy. The onset boundary is markedly asymmetric: current-sheet formation appears to be controlled mainly by damping of the magnetic potential, rather than by the combined damping strength. The analyticity strip collapses to the grid scale, the concentration sharpens under grid refinement, and the observed growth is consistent with an energy-critical self-similar rate, with exponent near three. These experiments indicate that magnetic-potential damping is the apparent binding constraint for current-sheet concentration, refining the symmetric sum picture.

papers.title: Label-Free Finite-Volume-Residual Training of Attention Graph Neural Networks for Coupled Thermo-Fluid Fields
papers.summary: Neural surrogates are widely used in scientific machine learning for fast prediction of three-dimensional (3D) thermo-fluid fields. However, generating training data using conventional numerical solvers often incurs substantial computational and storage costs. We propose to train an attention graph neural network by minimizing the finite-volume method (FVM) residuals of the governing equations. These residuals are evaluated directly on the mesh, requiring no labeled data. We evaluate the trained surrogates against computational fluid dynamics (CFD) references and a data-supervised baseline across four scenarios. On the two steady-state benchmarks, each solved on the same mesh as its CFD reference, the FVM-loss model reproduces the reference flow and temperature fields with mean field-averaged normalized root-mean-square errors (nRMSEs) near 3%, including the buoyancy-energy coupling. On the two parametric transient cases, the FVM-loss model attains lower rollout errors than the supervised baseline in almost every field, while avoiding the data-generation cost entirely. These results indicate that the FVM loss can provide a practical training signal for neural surrogates and reduce the model development cost.

papers.title: Design and Optimization of Metasurfaces for Silicon Photonics: PhD Thesis
papers.summary: Metasurfaces, two-dimensional arrangements of subwavelength nanopillars, provide local control over the phase of light, enabling flat optical functions beyond conventional refractive components. Their inverse design, finding the pillar distribution producing a target response, faces two obstacles: the immense dimensionality of the design space and the prohibitive cost of rigorous electromagnetic simulations, precluding exhaustive exploration at device scale. This thesis addresses the challenge in three stages. The first assesses the reliability of rigorous Maxwell solvers: comparing three implementations of Li's factorization rules for RCWA shows that spectral convergence does not guarantee physical fidelity, as these rules implicitly distort the simulated permittivity, most severely in the plasmonic regime. FDTD, immune to such artifacts, is retained as ground truth throughout. The second stage removes the computational bottleneck: a local phase-approximation model, then fully convolutional surrogates trained on FDTD simulations of large pillar metasurfaces, predict the near field almost instantaneously. Exploiting problem symmetries quadruples the training database, and the surrogates generalize to much larger apertures while remaining differentiable. The third stage benchmarks three strategies under a common FDTD protocol ($R^2$ between realized and target far fields): Gerchberg-Saxton retrieval and Local Model ($R^2\approx0.925$), surrogate-based and heuristic-initialized gradient descent ($R^2\approx0.975$), and a generative framework based on diffusion models and Schr\"odinger bridges. Hybrid posterior sampling and amplitude constraints restore scale-invariant fidelity on surfaces over 230 times larger than training, with diverse, fabrication-tolerant designs. Database enhancement lifts every approach to $R^2\approx0.97$.

papers.title: Interference between multiple photoionization pathways in chiral molecules: Converging continuum results in Gaussian bases
papers.summary: An accurate description of photoionization observables is a central challenge for theoretical models of molecular photoionization. Within standard electronic-structure approaches, the continuum states are represented by unoccupied Hartree-Fock orbitals expanded in Gaussian basis sets. Since these basis sets are optimized for bound states, computed observables may exhibit a noticeable basis-set dependence. Here, we augment these basis sets with diffuse functions and investigate the convergence of photoelectron circular dichroism (PECD), anisotropy parameters, and the forward backward ionization time delay in the multiphoton ionization of randomly oriented methyloxirane molecules. All observables converge systematically with the number of added diffuse functions, resolving previously observed basis-set discrepancies and indicating that the augmented basis sets provide a more accurate representation of the intermediate continuum states. In particular, our fully ab initio calculations yield forward-backward time delays in qualitative agreement with recent measurements, for which previous theoretical descriptions relied on empirical modeling. Diffuse augmentation thus provides a computationally efficient and transferable route to converged Gaussian-basis calculations for molecular multiphoton photoionization.

papers.title: Trapping: The "Waterfall" of Vlasov-Poisson Dynamics and the Post-Transient Emergence of Drift-Independent Hole Structures in Collisionless Plasmas
papers.summary: A key aspect of structure formation in collisionless plasmas is particle trapping or, more precisely, the gap this process leaves in the theoretical description. While the dynamics prior to the onset of trapping are governed by Landau physics and phase mixing, the full effects of nonlinearity only emerge during the trapping phase, for which an explicit description is lacking. Consequently, this gap divides the temporal evolution into a linear Vlasov-Poisson phase preceding the transition and a post-transient Vlasov-Poisson phase characterized by a wide spectrum of particle trapping scenarios and associated Schamel equilibria. Metaphorically, this trapping process can thus be compared to a waterfall in fluid dynamics, where, similarly, no explicit dynamic link can be established between the regions above and below the cascade. A second insight is that the Vlasov-Poisson mean-field description fails due to the separatrix singularity, which necessitates a temporary recourse to the BBGKY hierarchy. To resolve this problem of the singularity, an analysis using the method of matched asymptotic expansions is proposed. Applied to the singular boundary of the separatrix zone, this approach employs local smoothing techniques, such as those mediated by the two-particle correlation function. It offers a suitable mechanism for selecting hole equilibria in the post-transition phase. Furthermore, we report the existence of a spatially periodic Langmuir hole that vanishes if regularity requirements are too stringent, and we demonstrate that self-acceleration, accompanying the transition from a slow electron acoustic hole to a fast Langmuir hole, is driven by the release of particularly deeply trapped electrons.

papers.title: Parity-equivariant prediction of conformer-resolved electronic circular dichroism spectra accelerates absolute configuration assignment
papers.summary: Electronic circular dichroism (ECD) is a key experimental probe for assigning the absolute configuration of chiral molecules, but interpreting measured spectra often requires costly time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) calculations. The few existing machine learning methods for ECD prediction are faster, but their accuracy still falls well short of that required for experimental applications. Here we introduce PhysECD, a parity-aware E(3)-equivariant framework that builds the spectrum from its underlying quantum-chemical quantities, ensuring correct chiroptical symmetry by construction. To improve generalization and support experimental applications, we construct SCECD, a conformer-resolved dataset of 578,104 computed spectra spanning diverse natural products with one to five stereocentres. PhysECD predicts ECD spectra from conformer geometries in milliseconds, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the CMCDS benchmark and SCECD. Validation against 77 experimental spectra further demonstrates that PhysECD can serve as a fast alternative to TDDFT for assigning the absolute configuration of complex chiral molecules.

papers.title: Plasmon-polaritons in a rarefied nonrelativistic neutron gas
papers.summary: The electromagnetic properties of a dilute unpolarized nonrelativistic neutron gas are described in the case when neutron-by-neutron scattering is negligible. The Gaussian (Maxwell-Boltzmann) and Fermi-Dirac one-particle density matrices for the neutron gas are considered, the typical space scale of variations of these density matrices being assumed to be much larger than the typical space scale of variations of the electromagnetic field. The Green functions for the static effective Maxwell equations are obtained. It is shown that a rarefied neutron gas does not possess a ferromagnetic instability even in a nonequilibrium state. The analog of Friedel oscillations is described. The properties of plasmon-polaritons in the neutron gas are revealed. It turns out that the dispersion law of longitudinal and transverse plasmon-polaritons has an infinite number of branches at a given momentum. The region of parameters where the plasmon-polaritons can be regarded as quasiparticles is found. The plasmon-polaritons on a Gaussian wave packet of a single electron are described. Their dispersion law proves to have an infinite number of branches at a given momentum. It is shown that there exist stable longitudinal plasmon-polaritons even on a single electron.

papers.title: Explainable GeoAI for urban wildfire structure loss: vegetation and built environment in the 2025 Palisades Fire
papers.summary: Urban wildfire resilience depends on interactions among built form, vegetation condition, and extreme fire weather, yet city-scale risk models often overlook whether predictive skill transfers across neighborhoods. We developed a spatially validated GeoAI workflow for the January 2025 Palisades Fire, linking 12,081 CAL FIRE damage inspections to pre-fire Sentinel-2 vegetation indices, Landsat surface temperature, LANDFIRE fuels, terrain, and OpenStreetMap buildings and roads. Among 9,883 inspected residential structures, 5,566 were destroyed. Random cross-validation yielded ROC-AUC 0.92 for the integrated XGBoost model, but 1 km spatial block validation reduced performance to 0.75; logistic regression performed similarly and was better calibrated. Building count within 100 m was the strongest predictor, with destruction odds increasing 4.12-fold per standard deviation. Vegetation moisture and greenness showed opposing conditional associations: NDMI at 100-300 m was protective (OR 0.52), whereas NDVI at 30-100 m was positively associated with destruction after accounting for moisture (OR 1.74). Predictive information was concentrated at the 100-300 m neighborhood scale. A separate post-fire track mapped burn severity and vegetation recovery without leakage. The results support neighborhood-scale susceptibility screening, moisture-aware vegetation management, and spatial block validation as a minimum standard for single-event urban wildfire modeling.

papers.title: Multiphysics simulation of all-optical switching and sequential magneto-optic readout in an integrated Si$_3$N$_4$/GdFeCo waveguide
papers.summary: In an integrated all-optical magnetic device, a guided pulse writes a magnetic state and a later optical signal reads it out. We study both steps for an 8 nm GdFeCo film inserted across a Si$_3$N$_4$ waveguide. A three-dimensional dispersive finite-difference time-domain calculation gives the energy absorbed from an 800 nm pump pulse. This energy drives a four-temperature model and calibrated stochastic two-sublattice Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch dynamics. After relaxation, a separate 532 nm probe is propagated through the fixed magnetic state for the optical readout. At the reference pump fluence, the model reverses 0.859 of the film from either saturated state. The switched fraction remains within 0.81-0.87 over a 2.4-fold range of incident fluence. A threshold rule applied to the local absorption map reproduces the five three-dimensional simulation points to within $8\times10^{-4}$, showing that, within the model, incomplete reversal results from non-uniform guided-mode absorption. When the film starts from zero magnetization, thermal noise orients the recovered local moments at random; over 16 realizations, $0.502 \pm 0.004$ of the cells end with a negative $x$ component of the FeCo moment. Among the simulated states, the probe transmission, reflection, and absorption fractions vary by at most 0.02. The magnetic Faraday and Kerr rotations are much more sensitive and become about 12 and 130 times smaller, respectively, in the stochastically recovered state than in a saturated film. The reflected signal also contains a magnetization-independent geometric background, which can be removed by subtracting a reference signal. These results link the switching efficiency to the guided-mode absorption profile and predict polarization-based readout of the simulated magnetic states. The model assumes a homogeneous film and neglects spatial exchange stiffness and subsequent domain coarsening.

papers.title: Tsallis Holographic Dark Energy with varying Gravitational Constant vs $\Lambda$CDM : A Comparative Outlook
papers.summary: We investigate the cosmological evolution of a flat Friedmann--Robertson--Walker Universe filled with Tsallis holographic dark energy (THDE) under the assumption that the gravitational constant $G$ varies with time according to the power-law parametrisation $d\ln G / d\ln a = \alpha_G = \mathrm{const}$. In this framework, the holographic dark energy density is given by $\rho_{\mathrm{DE}} \propto L^{2\gamma - 4}$, where $L$ is the future event horizon and $\gamma$ is the Tsallis non-additivity parameter. We study both the past and future evolution of the Universe for various values of the model parameters $C$, $\gamma$, and $\alpha_G$. The viability of the model is tested against a combination of observational data, including the Pantheon+ Type Ia supernova sample, direct Hubble parameter measurements $H(z)$, and baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data. Using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and Bayesian analysis tools such as the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC), the Bayes factor, and the suspiciousness metric, we perform a rigorous statistical comparison with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model. Our results show that models with a varying gravitational constant are preferred over $\Lambda$CDM. The best fit to the combined data is obtained for the THDE model with $C < 1$. Furthermore, we analyse the internal consistency of the data sets using the Index of Inconsistency, the $Q_{\mathrm{DMAP}}$ statistic, and Bayesian suspiciousness. We find that the THDE model with varying $G$ and $C < 1$ partially alleviates the tensions between different probes, reducing the significance from $\sim 7.4\sigma$ to $\sim 5.3\sigma$.

papers.title: Recovering topological information of light by topological learning
papers.summary: The evolution of modern-day communication networks towards enhanced capacity and robustness is driving interest in topological light wave as a next-generation information carrier. However, harnessing its potential is hindered by the lack of an effective topological reader, particularly when strong disorder renders conventional readout intractable. Here we address this by introducing TOPO$^{2}$, an artificial intelligence framework that leverages on topological learning to recover topological information from light. We demonstrate it on highly distorted optical fields with embedded Skyrmion topologies, showing that we can extract the topological numbers in a single shot with just a conventional camera. We showcase its capability in a TOPO$^{2}$-based communication scheme, sending and recovering information encoded in a topological alphabet, confirming that it outperforms conventional approaches. Our connection of topological photonics with topological AI as a powerful paradigm for robust high-capacity information encoding and processing opens a new path towards topological information optics.

papers.title: Fundamental limits to identifying node and tie memory in temporal networks: marginal artefacts and spreading dynamics
papers.summary: Temporal-network models place the memory seen in contact data either on nodes, through self-excitation (branching ratio n_node), or on ties, through reinforcement (kappa). The two choices reproduce the same coarse statistics but predict different epidemics. We ask whether contact data can tell them apart and find two limits. The first is attribution. When the initiator of every event is recorded, the likelihood factorises into a timing block containing n_node and a selection block containing kappa, so the two are estimated independently. When it is not, as in proximity data, a missing-information term couples them, with a size set by the entropy of the initiator posterior. The second issue is interpretation. Even where the mechanisms separate, the fitted n_node might not accurately measure memory and it may be set by the distribution of waiting times between events. Shuffling each node's inter-event order, which keeps that distribution, typically changes the estimated n_node by less than 10%; this is a bias that longer records and a flexible scale-free kernel do not remove. Whether node memory is present must therefore be decided by model-free statistics, which find only weak order memory in the proximity records, far less than the fitted n_node around 0.9 would imply. Tie reinforcement remains recoverable, although a latent initiator inflates it by 28%-45%. The two limits lead to two recommendations: record who initiates each contact, and test a fitted node memory against shuffled and model-free benchmarks before interpreting it. On a high-school record, simulating from the fitted node memory under-predicts outbreak sizes by up to a factor of 2, whereas keeping tie reinforcement alone is closer at low transmissibility but overshoots at high.

papers.title: Machine learning kinetics from molecular dynamics data
papers.summary: Most molecular transitions occur on time scales far beyond direct molecular dynamics simulations. The committor, the probability that a configuration reaches a product state before a reactant state, is a central kinetic statistic, providing a mechanism-independent reaction coordinate and a foundation for transition path theory and the calculation of rates. This review surveys modern approaches for estimating the committor and related kinetic statistics from molecular simulations, with an emphasis on self-supervised methods that learn solutions of their defining dynamical equations rather than relying on labeled shooting data. We develop a common operator viewpoint connecting generator-based partial differential equations, variational principles, Markov state models, dynamical Galerkin approximation, and neural networks. Empirical and theoretical evidence points to the efficiency of these methods. We provide theoretical and practical guidance for realizing their full potential in applications, including strategies for treating non-Markovian effects and for sampling. We conclude by identifying opportunities for further research, including connections to reinforcement learning and generative modeling.

papers.title: Attosecond Charge Migration Induced by Core-Level Ionization: A Relativistic Real-Time Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Perspective
papers.summary: Core-ionization induced charge migration in molecular systems has been widely studied, but the influence of relativistic effects on such dynamics remains relatively unexplored from a relativistic theory perspective. This issue is particularly important because core orbitals exhibit strong scalar-relativistic and spin-orbit imprints, and these effects are further enhanced in heavy-element systems, where relativistic signatures also alter the valence orbitals. To address this, we formulate four-component Dirac-Coulomb and two-component atomic mean-field exact two-component Hamiltonian approaches for studying charge migration within real-time time-dependent density functional theory. The time-dependent induced electric dipole moment is used as a marker of the characteristic charge-migration time scales. We apply the method to nitrosobenzene (N $1s$ electron removal), iodoacetylene (I $2p$ electron removal) and interhalogen series (I $2p$, Cl $2p$ electron removal). For iodoacetylene, the charge migration timescale is relatively insensitive to the choice of Hamiltonian but they show weak relativistic phase and amplitude modifications. However, it would be misleading to conclude that relativistic effects are generally unimportant. In interhalogen systems, we observe significant deviations between relativistic and non-relativistic dynamics. These results demonstrate that relativistic signatures in core-ionization-induced charge migration are not determined by heavy-atom core ionization alone, but by the relativistic sensitivity of the valence orbital manifold that drives core-hole screening and charge redistribution. Moreover, consistently across all systems, we observe a delay in the emergence of the relativistic imprints.

Gain and dark count rates were indirectly measured from the characterized electrical parameters. Both technologies exhibit remarkable stability of most of the functional parameters across all dose levels, while dark current shows predictable increases significantly more pronounced under proton irradiation due to displacement damage. papers.title: Energy-selective control of noise-assisted multipulsing by weak optical seeding in the dissipative-soliton-resonance regime
papers.summary: We investigate how weak optical injection changes single-pulse operation in a laser in the dissipative-soliton-resonance regime. The energy scans show that a small injected field suppresses multipulsing and extends predominantly single-pulse operation to higher energies. Further increasing the seed power makes this extended range nonuniform: regions of enhanced multipulse formation alternate with regions of suppression. We analyze timing and optical-phase fluctuations of the injection field. At the lowest energies, these fluctuations cause continuous-wave and multipulse generation to dominate the laser output. At the highest energies, injection-field phase fluctuations promote multiple pulses, whereas time fluctuations suppress them. Deterministic calculations without noise or injection show that both single pulses and prepared pulse pairs can persist under the same settings. We show that the spectral entropy of a dissipative soliton reflects changes in individual pulse spectra and pulse interference. It characterizes the probabilistic transition between single- and multipulse regimes, but it does not, by itself, predict in detail which regime the laser will form. Together, the results connect the energy-selective action of optical injection to pulse formation and structure, while distinguishing persistence of a prepared pulse from its formation out of a background.

papers.title: A 2D autocorrelation-based frequency estimator reflecting spatial tissue distribution to improve Ultrasound H-scan tissue characterization
papers.summary: H-scan is a promising quantitative ultrasound technique that estimates the frequency content of backscattered signals and maps the estimated frequencies onto a red/blue color scale to reflect underlying tissue properties. Although it relies on matched filters tuned to different frequencies, the broad spectral bandwidth of ultrasound produces noisy, granular displays. Here, we introduce an adaptive frequency estimator designed to suppress the noise within homogeneous regions while preserving sharpness across tissue boundaries. The method combines 2D autocorrelation with a matched filter. In the first stage, a matched-filter-based estimation yields an a priori map of the spatial distribution of frequencies. The local heterogeneity of these estimates then defines a 2D weighting function that guides a second estimation stage. Drawing on the concept of Loupas's blood velocity estimator, we apply autocorrelation over a 2D spatial kernel to recover the axial frequency components, employing a weighted summation that accounts for the spatial frequency distribution within the kernel. We benchmarked the proposed estimator against conventional approaches, including the short-time Fourier transform, the H-scan matched filter, and standard autocorrelation, using both Field II simulations and in vivo data from human subjects with hepatic steatosis. In simulation, our adaptive estimator reduced the noisy texture in homogeneous regions while retaining clear boundary delineation, whereas the other estimators could achieve only one of these objectives. Applied to the in vivo human liver, the estimator improved H-scan image quality by lowering noise and enhancing the discrimination of steatotic liver from adjacent gallbladder and skin layers.

papers.title: Bayesian inference of non-Maxwellian distribution functions from collective Thomson scattering spectra
papers.summary: We investigate Bayesian inference of non-Maxwellian electron distribution functions from collective Thomson scattering (CTS) spectra. We represent distribution functions using multiple candidate models of different complexity and perform inference on synthetic spectra generated from known non-Maxwellian distribution functions. Our analysis demonstrates that a sufficiently flexible model can approximate the overall shape of the ground-truth distribution function. The most plausible model is identified based on model evidence, a statistical measure representing the probability to obtain the observed data given the model. When the candidates include the ground-truth model, the model evidence favors the ground-truth model. Without the ground-truth model as a candidate, the model evidence favors the candidate model with the fewest parameters that adequately approximates the data. The posterior probability density function of the most plausible model reveals the characteristic features and associated uncertainties of the underlying distribution function. The origin of the additional spectral peaks is attributed to a combination of modifications to the dispersion relation and reduced Landau damping. This enables the objective and data-driven identification of distribution functions directly from observed CTS spectra.

papers.title: Stellarators Linking Axisymmetric Mirrors Part 1: Coil Design, MHD Equilibrium, and Physics Metrics
papers.summary: We present a computational design study of a stellarator-mirror hybrid concept, Stellarators Linking Axisymmetric Mirrors (SLAMs), in which an optimized poloidally omnigenous (OP or QI) stellarator serves as the rotational-transform-generating element that links long, axisymmetric (circular cross-section) magnetic mirrors. Starting from an OP precursor configuration obtained from the DESC omnigenity database, we construct hybrid coil sets for field period nFP = 2 SLAMs by separating the OP modular coils along the device midplane and inserting axisymmetric planar mirror coils into the resulting gap. Field-line tracing shows that nested vacuum flux surfaces survive this extrusion across a range of mirror-section lengths, with the cross-section qualitatively preserved at the point where the mirror is inserted. We use the field-line tracing data to map the shape of a surface and use the GVEC fixed-boundary solver to calculate an ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equilibrium and evaluate physics metrics such as the neoclassical transport proxy ($\epsilon_{\rm eff}^{3/2}$), the vacuum magnetic well (W), and the gyrokinetic heat fluxes (Q), providing a first-principles analysis of such concepts using modern stellarator analysis tools.

papers.title: Is MOND an effect of cosmic frame-dragging \`a la Mach?
papers.summary: The physical origin of Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND), which predicts galaxy rotation curves via a single empirical acceleration constant $a_0$ without the need for dark matter, remains unknown. I propose a modified-inertia origin for both MOND's interpolating function and $a_0$ within a framework closely related to Gravitoelectromagnetism, the linearized limit of General Relativity. Following Sciama's model unifying gravity and inertia, which implements Mach's principle and the relativity of acceleration through gravitoelectric induction, I consider an idealized homogeneous universe undergoing constant Hubble expansion. I identify $a_0 \sim H_0^2R_u \sim c^2/R_u$ with the relative recession acceleration of cosmic matter near the horizon, which dominates the cosmological contribution. I show that this scale enters local inertial dynamics only when the relative acceleration of the universe becomes anisotropic and the Rindler horizon is comparable to or larger than the cosmic Hubble horizon, at accelerations of order $a_0$ and below. By the simplest Ansatz for the observer's acceleration-dependent causal volume, accounting for the interplay between the cosmic and Rindler horizons, I derive MOND's simple interpolating function as a modified inertia law without the need to insert it by hand or make any further ad hoc adjustments. Physically, the region brought into causal connection ahead of the accelerating observer by the deformation of the cosmic horizon contributes less inertial drag than is lost from the region removed behind him by the Rindler horizon. This proof of concept motivates the possibility that MOND arises from large-scale linear inertial frame-dragging induced by the expanding universe within General Relativity.

papers.title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
papers.summary: The extreme intensity of X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) pulses has enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to enable biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Building on improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to ~20 to 30 Angstrom, even though the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

papers.title: From Critical Transitions to Sustainability Transformations: Phenomena, Theory, and Applications Across Disciplines
papers.summary: There has been a recent surge in the use of terms describing systemic change processes across science, policy, and public debate. The associated change phenomena are often assumed to be abrupt and irreversible once critical thresholds are crossed. However, the interchangeable use of terms leaves definitions and the underpinning scientific theory unclear, which can lead to misconceptions about transition processes and potential impacts. Here, we present selected empirical examples representing phenomena of tipping points, regime shifts, critical transitions, phase transitions, social and socio-technical transitions, and sustainability transformations, together with their underlying theory derived from the broadly defined domains of physics and mathematics, Earth science and ecology, social sciences, and their interdisciplinary overlaps. We bring these fields into closer conversation, creating a shared understanding of each of the conceptual roots, phenomena, mechanisms, and specific applications. This can help steward the governance of social-ecological change towards more just and sustainable futures.

papers.title: Matrix-Free Resolvent Analysis for Large-Scale Aerodynamic Systems
papers.summary: Predicting transonic buffet requires resolving both flow stability and disturbance amplification. Resolvent analysis gives the amplification. However, each gain needs the solution of tens of linear systems with the shifted Jacobian and its adjoint. Sparse direct factorization, the usual route, is extrapolated to need more than $130$ TB for a three-dimensional jet with $4\times 10^{7}$ unknowns. For the stiff Reynolds-averaged operator of a transonic wing, iterative solution has been reported to stall on the adjoint system. To avoid the direct factorization and to converge the adjoint, we present a matrix-free resolvent framework in the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes solver ADflow that combines automatic differentiation, Krylov solution with subspace recycling, and Lanczos bidiagonalization, with backward-error checks on each singular triplet. A three-level study of the NASA Common Research Model wing reaches $1.73\times 10^{8}$ complex unknowns. The coarsest grid predicts an unstable buffet mode, whereas no unstable eigenvalue is found on the finer grids within the shifts searched. The finer-grid gain peaks are consistent with collective amplification by damped modes, whose responses retain the buffet-cell structure and travel outboard at approximately $0.3$ of the free-stream speed. The peak gain remains sensitive to resolution despite these similar structures. These findings motivate future mesh adaptation targeted at convergence of flow stability and disturbance amplification.
