papers.title: $R_{\rm e}$, or not $R_{\rm e}$: Developing $R_5\equiv R_{-2}$ as a scale radius for galaxy sizes, masses, and mass-to-light ratios
papers.summary: The effective half-light radius $R_e$ marks an arbitrary 50-per-cent light boundary, and scaling relations involving such `effective' radii and their associated surface brightnesses, $\mu_e$, systematically (and undesirably) vary as the percentage changes. Here, the projected radius $R_5\equiv R_{-2}$, where the logarithmic slope of the surface-brightness and intensity profile equals 5 mag/dex and -2, respectively, and where the luminosity per logarithmic radial interval is maximal, is developed as an alternative. It can be measured non-parametrically or with a parametrized fit. For the S\'ersic $R^{1/n}$ family, $R_5=(2n/b_n)^nR_e$, with $R_5/R_e$->e$^{1/6}\approx$1.181 as n->$\infty$. Reparameterizing the (now $b_n$-free) $R^{1/n}$ model in terms of $R_5$ and $\mu_5$ removes the non-linear $R_e$-n coupling, and because the local slope is 5 mag/dex at $R_5$, correlated measurement errors in $R_5$ and $\mu_5$ better cancel when deriving the inferred total magnitude ($\propto\mu_5-5\log R_5$). Additionally, an exact single-integral identity is provided to relate any projected light percentage to the percentage within a sphere of the same radius. The scale radius $R_5$ is shown to be connected, through a weakly n-dependent factor to the anisotropy-insensitive internal radius $r_{-3}$, yielding a refined n-dependent Wolf-type mass estimator $M_{-3}$ and spatial mass-to-light ratio $(M_{dyn}/L)_{-3}$. Specifically, $M_{-3}\approx4G^{-1}R_{-2}\approx4.72G^{-1}R_e$. Past half-light substitutions in dynamical mass estimators introduce systematic S\'ersic-dependent offsets of 12-18 per~cent in enclosed mass and offsets spanning >20 per~cent in the mass-to-light ratio within $r_{-3}$. Dynamical mass estimators appropriate for (dark matter)-free stellar systems are also provided, and all relations are implemented in the companion Python package R5Tools.

papers.title: A Similarity Theorem and Its Breakdown in Atomic Black Hole Accretion
papers.summary: Inferring black-hole mass and growth from radiation processed by dense atomic gas requires connecting the emitting atmosphere to its feeding flow. We derive an exact similarity for point-mass accretion and use its limits to identify spectral information and dynamical consistency tests. At fixed temperature and composition, scaling mass, radius, and time together while scaling density inversely preserves the dimensionless flow, optical depths, and normalized spectra within a specified class of two-body microphysics, radiation, and boundary laws. Luminosity scales with mass, and the full atomic cooling curve is retained. Within this class the fixed-velocity power-law rescaling is unique. Density-sensitive populations and thermal radiation break the symmetry; public models of Little Red Dots illustrate the resulting density information. Even with luminosity and density normalization known, a prescribed spherical inflow retains an exact degeneracy between central mass and inward drift. A proposed feeding model nevertheless supplies growth and inventory tests. For point-mass Bondi feeding at fixed ambient sound speed, luminosity and its conversion to retained growth determine the ratio of adjustment to growth time independently of black-hole mass. For the critical isothermal Bondi profile with full retention, comparable times require gas mass comparable to the hole's mass. More generally, steady spherical continuity links luminosity and gas transit time to a required reservoir mass and minimum radial column. Lower retention slows growth while leaving this inventory unchanged at fixed supply and transit time.

papers.title: Primordial Black Hole Seeds for Little Red Dots in $f(R)$ Gravity
papers.summary: The little red dots (LRDs) discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope host black holes of up to $10^{9}\,M_{\odot}$ within the first billion years, posing a challenge to conventional seeding scenarios. We investigate whether such seeds can form in dense clusters of primordial black holes (PBHs), in which the central object grows by gravitational capture of the surrounding PBHs while accreting gas, within Hu-Sawicki $f(R)$ gravity, where the scalar field acts on the matter surrounding the PBHs. For the adopted cluster configuration, our results show that accretion and mergers reinforce one another: for time-averaged Eddington ratios $\lambda_{\rm Edd}\gtrsim0.3$, the seed consumes its cluster by $z\simeq5.5$-$7.3$ and subsequently grows into the LRD mass range. Calibrated on the observed black-hole mass function, the model reproduces the abundance of LRDs near the peak of their population without further adjustment, while it underpredicts the abundance at $z\simeq7.5$ and overpredicts it at $z\simeq2$. Our findings indicate that the earliest seeds may accrete about twice as efficiently as later ones, and that the finite cluster reservoir can imprint a lower edge on the mass function near the cluster mass. Within the adopted screening and halo-growth prescriptions, the scalar field enhances the abundance of active seeds by up to $\sim 13\%$ at lower redshifts and by $\sim 7\%$ at $z \simeq 7.5$ for the strongest model considered, modestly moving the high-redshift prediction towards the data at fixed normalization. Also, the remnant spins can further discriminate between feeding modes.

papers.title: STOKES tables and KY codes
papers.summary: The family of KY codes is an XSPEC-compatible package of fully relativistic models for spectro-polarimetric modeling of X-ray binary systems and active galactic nuclei. Within Kerr space-time, they compute accretion disc line profiles, reflection spectra from discs illuminated by Comptonized coronal radiation, and thermal disc emission including disc-corona interaction and disc self-irradiation. Many of these models include polarimetric computations, and more advanced timing variants compute X-ray, UV and optical reverberation. The primary source of Comptonized X-rays is assumed to be in the lamp-post on-axis or slab above the disc geometry. The KY codes operate at various levels of complexity; some models use analytical approximations for local re-processing, while others rely on detailed numerical tables. For the most accurate treatment of rest-frame re-processing in partially ionized accretion disc atmospheres, the KY codes employ pre-computed spectro-polarimetric tables generated with the STOKES code. These transmission and reflection tables are also designed for standalone use in XSPEC and as inputs to higher-level models beyond KY. The chapter first introduces the STOKES tables in various variants and shows their non-relativistic usage in XSPEC models for (i) an extended source illuminating a distant geometrically thin disc, and (ii) a compact source illuminating a vertically extended equatorial obscurer (e.g., a torus or thick wind). The relativistic KY ray-tracing is then described, followed by an introduction to each KY model. Examples of fits to the IXPE data of X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei using these models are shown. Together, these models form a comprehensive and publicly available framework for spectro-polarimetric modeling and data fitting of accretion. We provide links to their online repositories.

papers.title: A Kinematic Measurement of the Effective Viscosity of the Intracluster Medium: The Cold Front of A3667 Seen by XRISM
papers.summary: Constraints on the effective viscosity of the intracluster medium (ICM) come almost exclusively from imaging: the power spectrum of X-ray surface brightness fluctuations, and the morphology of Kelvin-Helmholtz rolls at cold fronts. Both indicate a viscosity below the isotropic Spitzer value. XRISM/Resolve opens a complementary, purely kinematic route, in which the viscosity is inferred from the thickness of the viscous shear layer that develops at a sliding contact discontinuity. We apply it to the prototypical cold front of A3667. The interface is the classical Rayleigh problem, in which momentum diffuses to a depth d in a time T, giving a kinematic viscosity \nu ~ d^2/(4T). The XRISM velocity map shows a line-of-sight velocity jump of 535 km/s across the front, completed within the 100 kpc-wide region immediately inside it, the only region with an anomalously broad line. Hence d ~< 100 kpc. Adopting interaction times set by the sizes of the interacting regions divided by this velocity, we obtain dynamic viscosities of 5.2 x 10^3 and 3.3 x 10^3 g/cm/s for the cool and the hot side of the front, or 6.4 and 0.72 times the Spitzer value. Because d is limited by the angular resolution of XRISM, and the viscosity scales as its square, these are upper limits. The kinematic constraint is consistent with, and independent of, the imaging results.

papers.title: Late-Time Emergence of Dark Energy and Its Interaction with Dark Matter
papers.summary: We present an interacting scenario between dark energy (DE) and dark matter (DM), where DE has an emergent nature, that means, DE was absent in the early universe but it becomes effective only at late times. We consider two specific emergent DE models, one with no free parameters and the other featuring two parameters describing the speed and epoch of the transition. We constrain both scenarios using the cosmic microwave background (CMB) measurements from the Planck 2018 release, baryon acoustic oscillations from DESI DR2, and three different compilations of Type Ia supernovae (PantheonPlus, DES-Dovekie, and Union3). Our analysis indicates that current cosmological probes are not able to tightly constrain the speed of the transition. For both scenarios, the posterior distribution of the interaction parameter is shifted away from zero at more than 95\% CL whenever the CMB data are combined with any of these additional probes, with the preferred direction corresponding to a transfer of energy from DE to DM. While CMB alone yields a high value of $H_0$, in agreement with local determinations, this effect is reduced when DESI is added and disappears once supernova data are included. In contrast, the clustering parameter $S_8$ is consistently shifted toward lower values in the combined datasets, and it is correlated with the preference for a negative interaction. However, according to the $\Delta \chi^2_{\rm min}$ and Bayesian evidence, none of the interacting models is favored over $\Lambda$CDM or $w_0w_a$CDM, indicating that the interaction does not rescue these emergent DE models. Our results therefore highlight the limitations of these scenarios in addressing current cosmological tensions, while pointing to the crucial role of future data in further assessing their viability.

papers.title: Hidden structures in the UHE sky: unveiling potential cosmic-ray sources via spectral signatures
papers.summary: The search for the origin of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) typically relies on identifying directional excesses in the particle flux. While this approach is well established, it cannot detect localized spectral features, which could provide constraints on the sources of UHECRs if measured. In this work, we propose extending directional searches through two complementary energy-weighted metrics: the accumulated energy $U$ and the local average energy per particle $\mu_E$. We demonstrate that $U$ inherently amplifies the statistical significance of sources with high-energy tails, while $\mu_E$ provides a distinct probe for direction-dependent spectra. To assess the statistical significance of these metrics, we derive a generalization of the Li-Ma significance formula for continuous energy variables. Using a maximum-likelihood analysis within an exploratory Monte-Carlo model, we show that these variables can enhance discovery potential by amplifying localized excesses and identifying hard-spectrum regions that are not apparent in standard particle-flux maps, thereby providing a comprehensive probe of potential UHECR sources. Furthermore, $\mu_E$ variations associated with localized excesses are smoothed into minor perturbations when the spectrum is integrated over right-ascension or declination bands. Consequently, the presence of small- or intermediate-scale regions with distinct spectral shapes remains consistent with the absence of declination-band spectral variations recently reported by the Pierre Auger Collaboration.

papers.title: The Neutral Hydrogen Gas Content of Star-forming and Quiescent S0 Galaxies
papers.summary: Lenticular (S0) galaxies that remain actively star-forming (SFS0s) are a unique transition population among galaxies. We investigated the HI (21cm) neutral hydrogen content of a sample of lenticular galaxies identified from within the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory (MaNGA) survey and which have been classified as star-forming or quiescent (qS0s). We compared these populations to each other and to a sample of star-forming spiral (SFSp) galaxies in MaNGA. We found that the HI mass fraction and HI deficiency of the SFS0s were intermediate between the qS0s and the SFSps, but more similar to the spirals. The HI depletion time of the qS0s is very much longer than that of the SFS0s and spirals, which have roughly similar times. We also compared the molecular gas fractions of the three groups which shows that the lowest fraction of the three populations is found in the qS0s, followed by the SFS0s and then the SFSps. A comparison of total baryonic mass indicates that the SFS0s have significantly lower masses than the qS0s in the sample. This suggests that the SFS0s must form from lower mass progenitors (unobserved by MaNGA) which either accrete external gas or lose spiral arms. The more massive qS0s are a completely separate population, most likely to be formed either from fading SFSps or from medium- to high-mass spirals undergoing mergers. The SFS0s in this sample cannot form from the qS0s in this sample that receive in-falling gas, nor can they fade to create these qS0s.

papers.title: Forward Bayesian Inference for the Binary Black Hole Populations
papers.summary: We present PopCWB, a Bayesian framework for the inference of the binary black hole (BBH) population based on the unmodeled search pipeline coherent WaveBurst (cWB). The standard population analysis takes an inverse approach by inferring the underlying population model parameters for a given set of detected events using the individual posterior samples. In PopCWB, we take a forward approach to population inference by varying population models to identify the most optimal one which describes the observed events. Rather than using event-level posterior samples, PopCWB uses a large set of simulated events reconstructed by cWB and their total mass, estimated with a machine-learning regression, to construct marginal probability distributions. These marginal probabilities are then used in the construction of the likelihood. We apply PopCWB to BBH events detected by cWB during the third observing run (O3) of the LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA detectors. We constrain an astrophysically motivated BBH population model that incorporates the effects of pulsational pair-instability supernovae and dynamical mergers. The analysis predicts a maximum black hole mass of $\mathbf{45.5^{+5.1}_{-6.1} M_{\odot}}$ from stellar evolution and an inferred local BBH merger rate of $\mathbf{23.0^{+16.6}_{-8.3} \, Gpc^{-3} yr^{-1}}$. We compare these results with the existing population models from the literature.

papers.title: The Dancing Bonfire: An Unusual Persistent X-ray Source in M81 Exhibiting Recurrent Luminous Flares
papers.summary: Short-timescale X-ray variability provides a direct probe of unstable accretion onto compact objects, yet extragalactic X-ray binaries (XRBs) with recurrent flaring remain largely unexplored. Here we present a detailed X-ray study of M81F4 (2CXO~J095524.2+690957), a persistently luminous X-ray source towards M81 that exhibits recurrent short X-ray flares. Based on multi-mission X-ray observations spanning two decades, it is found that M81F4 remains persistently bright at $L_{0.5-8.0\rm~keV}\sim10^{38}-10^{39}\rm~erg~s^{-1}$, while producing flares lasting a few hundred seconds and reaching peak luminosities of a few $10^{39}\rm~erg~s^{-1}$, with an observed mean (minimum) recurrence time of $\sim0.5$ day ($\sim$6 ks). The stacked flare profile shows a rapid rise followed by a slower decay, but no significant hardness evolution. Spectral analysis reveals that both the flare and non-flare states are dominated by a hard power-law continuum, with marginal evidence of highly ionized Fe lines in the non-flare state spectrum. These properties disfavor classical Type I and Type II bursts and have no close analog among known XRBs. We favor a magnetized neutron star accreting from an intermediate mass donor at a persistently high rate with the flares arising from instabilities at the disk-magnetosphere boundary. If confirmed, M81F4 might represent a hidden population of XRBs in which sustained, magnetically-regulated accretion can lead to brief episodes of super-Eddington emission.

papers.title: Clustering of JWST LRDs. Implications for PBHs and other early-forming seeds
papers.summary: We use the observed abundance and spatial clustering of JWST little red dots (LRDs) over z = 4--8 to confront two formation scenarios: the standard picture in which LRDs form in virialized dark-matter halos, and one in which they are seeded by a dynamically subdominant population of primordial black holes (PBHs). The halo formation scenario accounts for both observables naturally and without fine-tuning. In the PBH scenario, matching the observed LRD abundance requires a negligibly small PBH mass fraction, and a power-spectrum analysis shows that such a Poisson isocurvature component predicts a clustering signal far below what is observed. The same conclusion holds for any population of dynamically subdominant early-forming seeds, unless their initial clustering is finely tuned or their activity is tied to massive host halos. We conclude that the spatial clustering of JWST LRDs strongly favours the standard halo formation picture and disfavours PBHs, or similar early-forming seeds, as a randomly activated LRD population; PBHs remain viable as seeds only if their activity is governed by massive host halos, in which case clustering alone cannot distinguish them from astrophysical seeds.

papers.title: MACE: Multigroup-Multiangle Integrated Thermal Compton Scattering Kernel
papers.summary: We present a comprehensive set of accurate Compton-scattering tables for use in multigroup, multiangle radiation-transport calculations. The tables contain the exact thermal Compton kernel integrated over incident-energy groups, scattered-energy groups, and angular bins. To generate them, we develop a deterministic integration method in which the pointwise kernel is evaluated with a robust numerical treatment that remains accurate across challenging regions of parameter space. The multidimensional integrals are computed using nested quadratures whose panels adapt to the Compton recoil ridge, its thermal broadening, and the nearly elastic forward-scattering boundary layer. We validate the tabulated results against published kernel profiles, angular and energy moments, mean free paths, multigroup redistribution data, and an independent Monte Carlo estimator. The resulting tables provide the radiation-transport community with accurate, reproducible, and readily usable Compton redistribution matrices and angular moments.

papers.title: Rest-frame Ultraviolet Variability of Quasars in the Cosmic Himalayas Overdensity
papers.summary: Some high-redshift overdensities show an enhanced incidence of AGNs, suggesting that large-scale environment may influence supermassive black hole fuelling and triggering. Whether environment also affects AGN variability remains unclear. Using the Cosmic Himalayas (CH), an extreme concentration of 11 type 1 quasars at z=2.16-2.20, we investigate possible offsets in rest-frame ultraviolet variability relative to quasars with comparable redshifts, black hole masses, and Eddington ratios. We construct a parent sample of 1,138 Stripe 82 quasars at 2.11<=z<=2.25 and combine photometry from the SDSS, the PS1, and the ZTF to build observer-frame g- and r-band light curves spanning up to 27~yr. We compare DRW parameters and ensemble structure functions (SFs) with control pseudo-samples matched in black hole mass and Eddington ratio, and use injection--recovery simulations to forecast the detectability of a CH-like offset. The CH quasars show a tendency toward shorter DRW damping timescales (median offsets of -0.32 and -0.13 dex in g and r) and slightly higher asymptotic amplitudes. None of the four DRW comparisons is statistically significant, including the largest offset in the g-band damping timescale (p=0.16). Ensemble SFs generally exceed matched-control medians, although 18 of 19 lag bins per band remain within the 95% pointwise envelopes. Assuming a true uniform -0.32 dex g-band timescale offset, injection--recovery simulations predict an 80% probability of nominal 3sigma detection with approximately 60 quasars of comparable variability scatter and data quality. If confirmed, the tentative variability offsets may suggest that large-scale environment influences accretion-flow variability beyond its potential role in quasar triggering. Larger samples with higher-precision light curves, such as those expected from the LSST, are required to test this possibility.

papers.title: The first selection of optimal targets for the Lazuli ExtraSolar Coronagraph's reflected starlight exoplanet campaign
papers.summary: Direct detection and characterization of exoplanet atmospheres via reflected starlight enables probes of composition of mature exoplanet systems (since flux is decoupled from age) at closer separations than via thermal emission (due to observations in visible wavelengths), and even probes of biosignatures. New and upcoming ground and space-based platforms are enabling these observations for the first time. Recently the 3-m Lazuli Space Telescope, from the Eric and Wendy Schmidt Observatory System, was announced, which will be equipped with the ExtraSolar Coronagraph (ESC) designed for reflected light gas giant exoplanet observations in visible wavelengths. In this paper we present 27 known giant exoplanets that could make up an optimal first target list for these observations. This target list spans ages and temperatures of planets not probed before by direct imaging, but some of which will also be accessible to the \textsl{Nancy Grace Roman} Coronagraph instrument and the ELT-METIS thermal imager, providing comprehensive atmosphere characterization and synergies. We discuss the science enabled by ESC observations of this target list and enhancements provided by future astrometric and radial velocity measurements.

papers.title: A systematic evaluation of vision-language models for observational astronomical reasoning tasks
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly proposed as general-purpose tools for scientific data interpretation, yet their reliability on real astronomical observations across diverse modalities remains untested. We present AstroVLBench, a benchmark of over 4,100 expert-verified instances across five tasks spanning optical imaging, radio interferometry, multi-wavelength photometry, time-domain light curves, and optical spectroscopy. We systematically evaluate six state-of-the-art frontier models and find that performance is strongly modality-dependent and uncorrelated with general benchmark rankings. Mechanistic cross-model ablations reveal three concrete bottlenecks. First, prompt grounding exhibits marked model and task dependence: physical guidance yields more balanced classifications on optical imaging, whereas phenomenological prompts better navigate undersampled time-domain data. Second, presenting one-dimensional measurements as numerical tables rather than rendered plots consistently improves light-curve classification across all models by up to 23 percentage points, demonstrating that plot rendering can obscure physically relevant signal. Third, an expert audit of optical spectroscopy reveals a notable "right-answer-wrong-reason" phenomenon: across evaluated models, an average of 26% of correct predictions are accompanied by physically inconsistent or invalid reasoning chains, showing that accuracy alone is insufficient for trustworthy scientific deployment. AstroVLBench provides the first systematic, multi-modal baselines for VLMs in observational astronomy and identifies the representation, grounding, and reasoning bottlenecks that must be addressed before VLMs can be trusted as autonomous scientific interpreters.

papers.title: Population-level correlations in Bayesian statistics: an illustrative model for gravitational-wave astronomy
papers.summary: With increasingly large numbers of gravitational-wave events, population inference is now beginning to move beyond predictions of marginal distributions and to probe correlations between compact-binary parameters such as masses, spins, and redshifts. These correlations have strong constraining power for both astrophysics and tests of general relativity. In this paper, we present an idealized analytical model to study the interplay between single-event correlations, systematic biases, and population-level correlations. With this, we investigate the potential emergence of false-positive measurements of population-level correlations. We quantify how the presence of correlations at the single-event level between a pair of parameters increases the uncertainty of population-level correlations for those parameters, potentially obscuring the true underlying population correlation if present. We also find that if waveform systematics lead to biases that are correlated across the catalog (which is likely, because certain regions of the parameter space are more difficult to model), this can be effectively absorbed by a population analysis that targets correlations and can be misinterpreted as such. This simple Gaussian-based model may serve as a broad compass for future, more detailed explorations.

papers.title: Time-domain framework for the Teukolsky equation with a particle source using comoving hyperboloidal coordinates
papers.summary: We present a scheme and implementation code for time-domain integration of the Teukolsky equation in 1+1 dimensions with a point-particle source, based on comoving, spatially compactified hyperboloidal coordinates. We demonstrate that the scheme evades the problem of nonphysical growing modes that plague some numerical evolution schemes without compactification. Our use of comoving coordinates greatly simplifies the application of jump conditions on the particle's worldline. We develop our method and test its performance for a scalar field on a Schwarzschild background, first for a circular geodesic orbit source and then for a scattering geodesic orbit. We then present a test implementation of the method for the $s = -2$ Teukolsky equation, illustrating its long-term stability and absence of growing-mode behavior through comparison with similar results using noncompactified characteristic coordinates. Our method paves the way to calculations of the full gravitational self-force in extreme-mass-ratio scattering.

papers.title: Massive boson stars: Waveform-based branch diagnosis with neural reconstruction
papers.summary: We investigate whether the dynamical merger branch of massive boson-star collisions can be inferred from the gravitational waveform without supplying the intrinsic source parameters. Using an existing equal-mass, head-on numerical-relativity catalogue, we construct branch-conditioned reduced-basis surrogates for the real $(2,0)$ and $(4,0)$ modes and perform parameter-blind waveform inference. On a frozen test set of 60 held-out samples, the correct branch is recovered for all samples using either mode, showing that the branch information is not confined to the dominant $(2,0)$ channel. The inference also recovers $|\phi_c|$ with a mean relative error of $4.30\%$ and selects the correct $\lambda$ from $\{10,50,100,300\}$ in $68.3\%$ of the test samples. These results demonstrate waveform-based branch and source-parameter inference within the present noiseless numerical-relativity catalogue.

papers.title: Modified Cosmology from Mass-to-Horizon Relation: Observational Bounds
papers.summary: We constrain the class of modified cosmologies derived in Paper I [1] from a generalized mass-to-horizon relation (MHR) that enforces thermodynamic consistency between the Cai-Kim horizon temperature and generalized horizon entropies. The modified Friedmann equations depend on an entropy exponent $m$, an MHR coupling parameter $\gamma$, and an entanglement-correction amplitude $f_B$, with standard $\Lambda$CDM recovered in the appropriate limit. Using Pantheon$+$/SH0ES Type~Ia supernovae, cosmic chronometers, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations, and Planck 2018 CMB distance priors, we constrain eight physically motivated sub-cases via Markov chain Monte Carlo and compare models through the Bayesian log-evidence. The entropy exponent is tightly bounded, $|m-1|\lesssim O(10^{-4})$ when the MHR coupling is fixed ($\gamma=1$), relaxing to $O(10^{-3})$ along the $m$-$\gamma$ degeneracy, excluding any macroscopically significant departure from standard horizon thermodynamics. Freeing the MHR coupling parameter or the entanglement amplitude raises the inferred Hubble constant to $h\simeq0.70$-$0.71$, reducing the CMB-SH0ES tension from ${\sim}4\sigma$ to ${\sim}1.2$-$2.6\sigma$, but no scenario fully resolves it within a flat universe. The Bayesian log-evidence nevertheless disfavors every extension relative to $\Lambda$CDM in all dataset combinations ($-16\lesssim\Delta\ln Z \lesssim-1$): the improved fits obtained when the SH0ES calibration is included reflect an absorption of the Hubble tension by the additional parameters rather than genuine evidence for modified horizon entropy.

papers.title: The Bondi dipole in full numerical relativity: a self-accelerating positive-negative mass binary
papers.summary: Bondi showed in 1957 that a body of negative active gravitational mass and a positive one should accelerate together without limit while their total momentum stays zero. We test this prediction in full 3+1 numerical relativity, from constraint-satisfying initial data. The matter is two complex scalar fields with identical self-interactions, one of which enters the Einstein equations with the opposite sign; its stars have positive inertial and passive masses but negative active and Arnowitt-Deser-Misner (ADM) masses. To our knowledge, they are the first asymptotically flat bodies of negative ADM mass evolved in numerical relativity. A pair of stars with equal and opposite ADM masses accelerates as a single object at constant separation, and its total momentum stays zero to within 0.5%. The acceleration follows Newton's law of gravitation in both mass and separation, reverses when the stars are exchanged, and is absent in same-sign pairs and isolated stars. We detect no gravitational radiation. The results hold for head-on pairs released from rest, up to a few percent of the speed of light, and in the longest run the pair reaches a tenth of it with both stars intact.

papers.title: NRHJSur3dq8: a spectral numerical-relativity surrogate family for non-eccentric aligned-spin binary-black-hole waveforms
papers.summary: We present NRHJSur3dq8, a family of numerical-relativity surrogates for non-eccentric aligned-spin binary-black-hole waveforms inspired by an action-angle parameterization. The model provides both the dynamics: the Hamiltonian values, azimuthal action $J_\phi(\Phi)$, the orbital clock $\tau(\Phi)$ as functions of its phasing, and the radiative pieces: the waveforms, their near-analytic derivatives, and modeling errors associated with each. The surrogated variables are conditioned into pieces that vary slowly on the radiation-reaction timescale, represented on shared $h$-adaptive Chebyshev elements, and regressed across the intrinsic parameters with a Gaussian-process model. A time-parameterized merger-ringdown set of elements is attached where the adiabatic description breaks down. Fixed-hyperparameter leave-one-out validation of the central NRHJSur3dq8_AA model variant against numerical relativity gives a $(2,2)$ unweighted mismatch of $1.6^{+62}_{-1.5}\times10^{-6}$ and an all-mode mismatch of $2.8^{+84}_{-2.7}\times10^{-6}$ over the full inspiral-merger-ringdown span. Sky-averaged and signal-to-noise-ratio-weighted over $32$ orientations per simulation, the model's full inspiral-merger-ringdown in-sample mismatch against the SXS numerical-relativity simulations used for training is $8.9\times10^{-7}$ to $2.8\times10^{-5}$ across total masses $40$-$120 M_\odot$. Waveforms are hybridized using post-Newtonian waveforms. Beyond accuracy, NRHJSur3dq8 provides two capabilities uncommon in numerical-relativity surrogates: nearly analytic derivatives of the strain with respect to the physical parameters, and a calibrated Gaussian-process predictive uncertainty of the model. A full non-hybridized inspiral-merger-ringdown waveform evaluates in $12.5$ ms on a single CPU call. Batched evaluation takes $0.43$ ms per waveform at a batch of $4096$, measured at a starting frequency of $25$ Hz.

papers.title: Black Hole Spacetime Reconstruction from Galactic Rotation Curves: Thermodynamic Properties and Implications
papers.summary: We study how the dark-matter environment of a galaxy, reconstructed directly from its observed rotation curve, affects the black hole at its centre. Using the rotation curve of the spiral galaxy NGC\,5907, we construct a general-relativistic model of its halo. The halo has a positive, outward-decreasing density, satisfies the null energy condition, and reproduces the galaxy's dynamical mass of about $3.3\times10^{11}M_\odot$ within 30\,kpc. We then embed a central black hole in this halo and derive its horizon, Hawking temperature, entropy, heat capacity, photon sphere and shadow. Because the halo's gravitational field is weak, all these quantities differ from those of an isolated Schwarzschild black hole by less than one part in $10^{5}$. The heat capacity remains negative, so the black hole stays thermodynamically unstable. For a black hole of $10^{8}M_\odot$, the shadow would span about 0.6\,microarcseconds. Archival WISE infrared photometry confirms, as expected, that the black hole leaves no imprint on the galaxy's light on kiloparsec scales.

papers.title: A Framework for Automated Multi-Source Satellite Data Analytics and LLM-Based Report Generation
papers.summary: This paper presents the workflow for building an automated ArcGIS Pro tool using ArcPy to extract the Land Surface Temperature (LST) from Landsat 7, 8 and 9 datasets. The tool eliminates the need for manual band selection and repetitive raster computations by automating the multi-step workflow of radiometric calibration, NDVI-based emissivity correction, and thermal conversion. In addition to supporting batch and single-scene processing, the tool has an optional Large Language Model (LLM) for statistical result interpretation and reporting. Depending on batch size, the tool reduced the processing time from around 11-58 minutes when done manually to around 4-11 minutes using the tool. We tested the tool with data from Ras Al Khaimah (RAK) in the UAE, and the LST obtained for Ras Al Khaimah ranged from approximately 25C to 50C, demonstrating an accurate LST mapping compatible with the weather conditions of RAK. In summary, our tool reduces human errors and improves processing accuracy and efficiency for thermal and environmental remote sensing applications, in addition to providing an interactive LLM-based interface for result's interpretation.

papers.title: Binary Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes in 3+1 numerical relativity: mergers, fly-bys and gravitational waves
papers.summary: We present what are, to our knowledge, the first three-dimensional numerical-relativity evolutions of wormhole binaries: pairs of massive Ellis-Bronnikov wormholes held open by a phantom scalar field, whose energy density is nowhere positive. We construct constraint-satisfying initial data for single throats and for pairs, at rest and with orbital momentum, and evolve them with adaptive mesh refinement. An isolated throat is unstable: depending on the sign of a small perturbation, it collapses to a black hole or inflates, at the rate that linear perturbation theory predicts to within 1.9%. Two throats at rest repel when their scalar charges have the same sign and attract when the signs are opposite, with a strength ratio close to the scalar force law's prediction, so only opposite-signed pairs merge. A head-on collision forms a common horizon around both throats while they are still open. The horizon then loses 28% of its area as it absorbs the scalar field, and approaches the Schwarzschild radius of the pair's mass. Pairs that fly past each other form no horizon, and both throats inflate. Every encounter emits a short burst of gravitational waves and a scalar dipole wave of comparable, negative energy. An isolated collapsing throat rings at the quasinormal frequency of the black hole it becomes. No throat survives more than a few orbital periods, even when its initial perturbation is tiny, so these binaries do not inspiral. The results hold for one phantom-scalar model, equal masses, a single throat compactness and no spin.

papers.title: Strong-Field Gravitational-Wave Lensing from Ray-Traced Arrival-Time Surfaces
papers.summary: The diffraction integral formalism has been greatly successful in describing gravitational wave lensing effects in scenarios where the wavelength of the signal is comparable to the characteristic length scale of the lens, known as the wave optics regime. However, the assumptions required to construct its integrand break down as the source approaches the strong gravity region of a black hole lens. In particular, we are interested in the lensed signal from a binary (the source) near a massive black hole (the lens). We present a new formalism for obtaining low frequency corrections to sources being lensed in the strong field regime of gravity by leveraging the fact that null geodesics obey the Hamilton--Jacobi equations. In doing so, we are able to construct a time delay surface without relying on the thin lens approximation, and solve the diffraction integral for the resulting surface directly. For a stationary source at $10M$, deep in the strong field regime, when comparing the results with a relativistic wave scattering model, we find $6.5\%$ and $0.3\%$ agreement in the peak amplification and first diffractive fringe, respectively. Furthermore, we find a $< 1\%$ agreement with the amplitude of the point mass lens with a source at $10^4 M$ in the weak field, but noticeable dephasing between the peaks of the amplification function at higher frequencies. This work allows for clean interpolation between otherwise separate regimes, valid for sources from $\sim 6M \to \infty$. It provides a transparent, physically motivated framework for computing beyond-geometric optics lensing effects in the strong field regime.

papers.title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release
papers.summary: Computational gene-function prediction generates annotations at a scale that experimental characterization cannot match, yet substantial errors remain even among leading methods. Explicit error-controlled calibration for Gene Ontology (GO) prediction remains largely undeveloped. We introduce GoCo, a structure-guided framework that calibrates how scores from an existing predictor are converted into released annotations. GoCo certifies a global threshold for a GO-hierarchy-aware gene-level false discovery proportion (FDP), then constructs a nested release path under the same asymptotic risk-control guarantee. At the primary operating point (alpha=0.10, delta=0.50), GoCo-M, developed on Wainberg co-essentiality modules and applied without retuning to three independent studies with the same shared-evidence structure, kept mean held-out gene-level FDP at or below target while releasing 6.3-17.6% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel. For gene-specific neighbourhoods, GoCo-N orders individual calls. Developed on FunMap and validated without retuning on the STRING v12.0 experiments-only network, GoCo-N released 33.8% and 36.4% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel on the same refined score grid in FunMap and STRING, respectively, while keeping mean held-out FDP below target. The same pattern held under the stricter delta=0.10 setting. Thus, predictor-native biological structure can be reused at calibration, not only prediction, to release more supported annotations at a chosen gene-level error target without retraining the predictor.

papers.title: CausalOdyssey: Multi-Agent Local LLM Reasoning with Per-Patient Causal Structure for Rare Disease Retrieval
papers.summary: Patients with rare diseases often wait years for a diagnosis. Existing HPO-based retrieval tools narrow the differential to a shortlist, but a clinician reading that shortlist has no signal for which candidate to trust or what to test next. We present CausalOdyssey, a local four-agent pipeline on Gemma 4 26B built over a classical IC-weighted gene-rescue backbone: a Diagnostician reranks the slate via chain-of-thought over per-patient FCI causal edges and Reactome mechanism context; a Verifier computes deterministic evidence against the top-1 (missing pathognomonic phenotypes, pathway chain closure) and has Gemma issue a confirm/flag/refute verdict over it; an Interrogator selects one follow-up HPO by split-variance scoring; a Narrator emits citation-validated clinical prose. Only the Diagnostician changes the ranking; the other three agents annotate it. On RareBench n=1,122, reranking a top-30 slate lifts R@1 by +12.57 pp over our structural baseline ([+10.07, +14.97]; p=8.3e-24). A no-LLM variant of that baseline, without its inverse disease-count weight, reaches a similar pooled R@1 (36.3% vs 35.3%): the LLM rerank is far better on metabolic cases (RAMEDIS, +16.0 pp) and far worse on case-report corpora (LIRICAL, MME), so its value is corpus-dependent. We also propose a masked-phenotype protocol for evaluating follow-up suggestions without an annotation-based oracle; under it, the Interrogator asks for a patient's hidden phenotypes no more often than simple baselines (0.6% vs 1.2%), although a perfect follow-up would add 11 pp at top-1. The Verifier's verdict separates correct from incorrect top-1s (51.4% vs 12.1% top-1 accuracy under confirm vs refute). For 30% of patients the gold diagnosis is outside our top-30, though LIRICAL retrieves over half of these. All inference is local; no patient data leaves the machine. Demo code and a live demo are public.

papers.title: A Multimodal Machine Learning Framework Integrating Genomic, Epidemiological, Environmental, and Clinical Imaging Data for Accelerated Measles Detection and Transmission Inference
papers.summary: Background: Measles resurged in the United States during 2025-2026, with more than 4,600 reported cases. Timely detection and transmission inference require integrated genomic, epidemiological, environmental, and clinical data. We developed a multimodal machine learning (ML) framework integrating genomic sequences, epidemiological indicators, wastewater surveillance, and clinical rash images. Methods: We evaluated a three-stage pipeline using public data. Stage 1 classified transmission linkage among 903 sequence pairs from the 2021 Ohio-Arizona-Washington outbreak using k-mer TF-IDF-SVD embeddings and pairwise single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) distances with leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation. Stage 2 predicted state-week outbreak risk using logistic regression and XGBoost with wastewater, mobility, and vaccination features under leave-one-year-out cross-validation. Stage 3 used BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16 embeddings and a fine-tuned multilayer perceptron for rash classification on MSLD v2.0 (755 images, 6 classes). InfoNCE contrastive learning aligned genomic and imaging embeddings. Results: Transmission-linkage classification achieved AUC 0.924 and F1 0.912 with logistic regression. Outbreak-risk prediction achieved AUC 0.707 with logistic regression across 2025-2026 leave-one-year-out folds. Contrastive alignment achieved Recall@1 = 0.985 on held-out paired data. Ablation showed genomic features dominated transmission-linkage prediction (genomic-only AUC 0.983), whereas wastewater positivity was the strongest outbreak-risk predictor (importance 0.402). Conclusions: Multimodal ML integrating genomic, epidemiological, wastewater, and clinical imaging data can support measles surveillance and transmission inference using public data. Prospective validation with paired clinical-genomic data, expanded wastewater coverage, and real-world workflows is needed before deployment.

papers.title: ARMD-Predict: multi-site machine learning to predict antibiotic resistance before culture results
papers.summary: Clinicians select empiric antibiotics before culture susceptibility results are available. Electronic health record (EHR) models could inform that choice, but most are developed at a single hospital and transport poorly to others. We developed ARMD-Predict using 7.5 million culture-antibiotic observations from four academic medical centers. One set of models estimates susceptibility to individual antibiotics; a second, hierarchical set predicts the infecting organism and then organism-specific resistance phenotypes. Across 23 pooled susceptibility models evaluated in same-period, patient-grouped test partitions, median area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.77 for inpatient urine and 0.70 for inpatient blood cultures; chronological retraining reduced AUROC by approximately 0.04. At an exploratory threshold with 95% positive predictive value, derived and evaluated on the same test observations, the model identified 55% of ceftriaxone-susceptible inpatient urine observations as suitable for narrower therapy and flagged 60% of ceftriaxone-resistant observations for broader coverage. Organism classifiers achieved top-3 accuracy of 51.3-83.3%; phenotype AUROCs were conditional on the observed organism. Research applications are available at https://armd-predict.stanford.edu. Independent calibration, threshold and end-to-end prospective validation are required before clinical use.

papers.title: An Exploratory Multiome Analysis of a BCG-Associated HSPC Signature: Trained-Immunity Marker in Blood and an Adverse Prognostic Association in Tumour
papers.summary: Intravesical Bacillus Calmette--Gu\'erin (BCG) is an established treatment for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and recent evidence indicates that bladder BCG induces transcriptional and chromatin changes in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). However, the joint multi-omic structure of these BCG-associated changes and its potential to define transferable molecular signatures remain less well characterized. This study performed an exploratory integrative analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from two NMIBC patients sampled before and after BCG treatment. Following preprocessing and barcode-level integration, 653 HSPCs were analysed using Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA+) with 2,000 HSPC-specific variable genes and 25,000 variable chromatin-accessibility peaks. Of ten latent factors, Factor~1 showed the strongest association with BCG status ($r=0.495$) and captured variation across both molecular views. RNA weights from Factor~1 were used to derive candidate gene signatures that showed partial consistency across patient-specific models. Cross-context evaluation showed associations with overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and recurrence in GSE199471, while a subset of signature genes showed consistent directional changes in monocytes following BCG vaccination in GSE184241. Together, these findings identify a candidate multi-omic axis associated with BCG exposure and suggest that its derived molecular signatures exhibit context-dependent behaviour across distinct biological and clinical settings.

papers.title: Canonical residual physics-informed neural networks and algorithmic perturbation landscapes map cell-fate transitions in longitudinal H3K27M glioma
papers.summary: Pediatric high-grade glioma is a dynamically heterogeneous disease in which therapeutic selection pressures, microenvironmental selection and developmental plasticity can reorganize cellular-state structure over time. Here we investigated these adaptive behaviors in glioma dynamics from single-cell ecologies by merging physics-driven artificial intelligence and complex systems theory. Specifically, this study explores canonical residual-based physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), dynamical systems modelling comparators, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis to understand glioma cell fate decisions. The primary analyses distinguished longitudinal initial from recurrent H3K27M cells and, within the recurrent specimen set, stem/progenitor-like from differentiated/glial-like annotation-derived states. Across five-fold cross-validation, RD achieved AUC $0.995 \pm 0.005$ and macro-F1 $0.973 \pm 0.016$ for initial--recurrence discrimination, and AUC $0.698 \pm 0.012$ and macro-F1 $0.629 \pm 0.014$ for recurrent-state subtype discrimination. FP achieved AUC $0.931 \pm 0.018$ and $0.665 \pm 0.012$, respectively. Cross-model XAI repeatedly prioritized PTGDS, CHI3L1, IGFBP7, SPARCL1 and NRXN3 in longitudinal progression. BDM perturbation rankings emphasized heat-shock/stress-response and immune-associated network signatures. These findings are candidate computational network biomarkers rather than experimentally established causal signatures. The study provides a reproducible bridge between physics-constrained latent dynamics, interpretable gene attribution, and data-driven algorithmic perturbation landscapes for in silico pattern generation about glioma cell fate plasticity and early recurrence detection.

papers.title: Debate, Not Voting: Agentic Arbitration over Weak Optical Chemical Structure Recognition Models
papers.summary: Optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) turns a picture of a molecule into a machine-readable string, and it stands between decades of printed chemistry and any computational use. On real documents individual models remain unreliable. Over a 1000-molecule sample of MolParser, three readers score $46.0\%$, $43.4\%$ and $42.4\%$ exact match, yet at least one of them is right on $60.8\%$ of molecules. That gap is an ensembling problem, but not one voting can solve, because the readers seldom agree and seldom err together. We place the readers inside a multi-agent scaffold. Four language-model agents with cheminformatics tools argue about a candidate structure, write findings to an append-only knowledge base, and are held to render-and-compare gates that admit a correction only when it is demonstrably better. The debate reaches $61.9\%$, beating the best single reader by $15.9$ points and plurality voting by $9.2$ points ($p<10^{-9}$ for both, robust to correction for all $27$ tests we report), and is indistinguishable from the any-reader-right ceiling. That aggregate hides two opposing effects. On the $661$ molecules with no stereochemistry the debate is $3.9$ points above the ceiling ($p=0.004$), constructing structures no reader proposed, while on the $339$ stereochemical ones it falls below. We then swap the arbitrating model. A stronger arbitrator adds $2.2$ points (nominal $p=0.039$; neither this nor the $+3.9$ survives Bonferroni correction over all $27$ tests, so both are suggestive), and its mechanism is visible: it opens a correction on $423$ of $1000$ molecules against $120$, and an interaction test indicates it depends less on the readers (nominal $p=0.018$, not correction-robust). We conclude that the useful unit of progress is the arbitration policy rather than the reader, and that OCSR accuracy is better read against the union oracle than against the best single model.

papers.title: TargetAgent: Mathematical AI Co-Scientist for Drug Target Identification
papers.summary: Given the challenges of pharmaceutical development, there is increasing interest in computational approaches for identifying novel drug targets. Transcriptomics technologies enable the analysis of disease mechanisms at unprecedented resolution, while spatially resolved platforms further preserve the spatial organization of cells within tissues, allowing analysis to focus on specific regions of disease localization. To derive actionable therapeutic targets from these data, it is necessary to identify mechanisms that recur across a population rather than those observed in individual patients, which requires integrated analysis across disease conditions and donor cohorts. Here, we present the groundwork for an AI co-scientist framework for the sequential analysis of multi-batch spatial transcriptomics data that integrates interpretable mathematical models, including optimal transport, tensor factorizations, and topological data analysis, with LLM-powered agentic interpretation. Leveraging the complementary information provided by these mathematical models, the agents sequentially identify regions in which the disease is localized, molecular targets within these regions, and the direction in which each target should be modulated. Applied as a proof of concept to a public Stereo-seq study of the Alzheimer's disease (AD)-affected prefrontal cortex, we demonstrate that the agents converge on the white matter as the primary locus of the moderate-disease signal and identify a loss of myelin programme usage despite increasing oligodendrocyte abundance. The agents subsequently propose 29 candidate therapeutic targets, led by an oligodendrocyte differentiation module on which multiple mathematical perspectives converge, and flag 20 genes whose relevance to AD has not been previously reported. These results are hypothesis-generating and motivate further validation in larger, independent cohorts.

papers.title: RADAgent: Automating RADseq Pipelines with Private Open-Source LLMs
papers.summary: Restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) is a family of reduced-representation sequencing methods. It uses restriction enzymes to sample subsets of the genome, therefore allowing multiple individuals to be sequenced and genotyped together at low cost. RADseq is widely used for population genomics, evolutionary biology, marker discovery, and the development of SNP panels, but complete analysis still requires expert coordination across multiple tools and processing stages. Traditional RADseq analysis requires expert coordination of heterogeneous bioinformatics tools, intermediate artifacts, quality-control checks, and parameter-dependent decisions across multiple stages. Although individual steps can be scripted, executing the complete workflow still requires human oversight for state tracking, result validation, and failure handling. To automate this expert-driven coordination, we present RADAgent, which introduces a modular agentic method for reliable RADseq workflow execution with an open-weight LLM. RADAgent maps the natural boundaries of the RADseq workflow into 16 independently executable and verifiable agent modules and uses a model-independent runtime for bounded tool execution, on-disk verification, and failure recovery. We evaluate RADAgent on a real population-genomics dataset containing 476 samples from 19 populations. The results demonstrate that RADAgent reliably automates the complete RADseq workflow with an open-weight LLM while keeping genomic data and model execution within the local computing environment. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/wenlu-lab/RADAgent.

papers.title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data
papers.summary: Researchers often pool public gut microbiome datasets from immunotherapy studies to get around small sample sizes, assuming that adding cohorts adds statistical power faster than it adds differences between studies. We test that assumption. We processed four public shotgun metagenomic cohorts of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade through one pipeline and pooled them step by step, from 39 to 283 patients. Because the PERMANOVA effect size R^2 is above zero even when there is no real effect, we compared every result with its exact chance expectation. Measured as raw variance explained, cohort membership accounted for 8 to 27 times more variance than treatment response, although much of that ratio comes from sample size alone. At every pooling step, treatment response explained no more variance than chance (within 0.2 percentage points) and was never significant, while cohort membership explained 6.0 to 9.5 percentage points beyond chance (p = 0.001 each time). Classification stayed at chance across three model types, none of six leak-free batch-correction strategies recovered signal, and no genus reached significance in a random-effects meta-analysis. The largest single cohort (n = 165) was also non-significant, although simulation shows it had at least 90% power to detect an effect at its own 95% upper bound; within it, recruiting site alone explained 7.0 percentage points beyond chance. In three tumor genomic cohorts (n = 223), a small but real response effect sat next to a cohort effect about eighteen times larger, so the problem is not specific to microbiome data. We release batch_detector, an open tool that reports chance-corrected cohort and response effects before pooling, and test it on an independent colorectal cancer meta-analysis.

papers.title: Physiology as Topology: Intervenable Organ Graphs for Longitudinal Patient Forecasting
papers.summary: Do language models forecast patient trajectories by reasoning through physiology, or by fitting surface statistics? We introduce PhysioCircuit, a multi-agent agent system that represents each organ as an agent and each physiological relation as an editable mechanism card with direction, lag, and evidence. Its expert-defined graph is frozen at inference, enabling controlled edge interventions. We also introduce PhysioCircuit-Bench, a mechanism-controlled benchmark spanning three organ systems, treatment events, and real ICU admissions. We evaluate intervention-direction agreement (IDAR), which requires the affected organ to change in the expected direction within the expected lag window. The expert graph substantially outperforms all topology controls on edge-IDAR, including fully connected, random, and reversed graphs. Independent clinician adjudication supports the counterfactual results. PhysioCircuit transfers to new organ systems by configuration alone, without retraining, while preserving inspectable and editable relations.

papers.title: Duration-Aware World Models for Sleep Staging with Dwell-Time Constraints
papers.summary: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current stage has persisted for its minimum duration. Discriminative classifiers fragment stage trajectories---for example, a 30 s Wake segment inside a 10 min N2 run---and even hidden semi-Markov smoothing leaves 11.3% of segments below the minimum dwell threshold. This paper presents a world model in which a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns dwell structure endogenously from EEG, via duration-aware latent sampling, a survival-curve dwell prior, and transition-matrix calibration, and a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer guarantees the minimum dwell at decoding. On SHHS-1 (200 subjects, 160/20/20, three repeated splits), the model reaches a test accuracy of 0.690 +/- 0.053 (95% CI over 3 folds) versus 0.641 +/- 0.042 for an identically split discriminative baseline, with macro-F1 +17.5 pp and better accuracy on all three folds. On Sleep-EDF the constraint layer cuts below-threshold segments from 71.8% to 0.1% with no accuracy loss (0.734 to 0.737), and an online locked scheduler reduces RL policy switches by 87% per night while keeping every policy run at least 90 s. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first system to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

papers.title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
papers.summary: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median C\alpha RMSD of 0.37 \AA) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

papers.title: Multiscale Topology-Regulated Nonlinear Dynamics for Protein B-Factor Prediction and Single-Cell Type Classification
papers.summary: Protein B-factor prediction and single-cell type classification are important for characterizing structural variability and cellular heterogeneity, with applications in biological function analysis and drug discovery. However, static geometric descriptors do not directly capture how multiscale connectivity shapes responses to local perturbations. Here, we introduce multiscale graph-coupled Burgers response learning (MGCBRL), a framework integrating algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics to construct predictive biological representations. Specifically, a filtration converts protein coordinates or cellular principal component scores into weighted graphs at ten neighborhood scales. Independent unit impulses initiate node-specific responses governed by nonlinear Burgers dynamics. Statistical summaries or sampled source-node trajectories then encode the influence of structural neighborhoods on transient signal evolution. The simulated responses serve as computational probes rather than models of biological motion. For cross-protein prediction, multiscale response statistics are combined with spectral perturbation descriptors measuring changes in Laplacian spectra after node removal. For single-cell classification, principal component scores augment these features to retain explicit expression-space information, and the resulting descriptors support downstream supervised learning. Across 104 proteins and 13 single-cell datasets, MGCBRL achieved configuration-selected mean scores of 0.888 for within-protein Pearson correlation and 0.950 for transductive cell classification balanced accuracy, with leave-one-protein-out mean correlations of 0.496-0.558. Our framework provides a shared strategy for transforming multiscale biological connectivity into informative response descriptors, supporting predictive analysis of protein structures and transcriptomic profiles.

papers.title: ProtAgent: Post-Training Compact Protein Tool Agents with Interaction-Level Credit Assignment
papers.summary: Protein annotation agents must choose suitable bioinformatics tools, interpret their outputs, and use the resulting evidence in the final answer. Most existing systems rely on frontier-scale models. We ask whether a compact model can instead learn this behavior through post-training with real tool interaction. We present ProtAgent, a two-stage pipeline that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the tool interface and standard on-policy REINFORCE to improve the interaction policy. Intermediate tool calls receive action rewards, and the final response receives a terminal answer reward. Step-level returns assign these rewards to the responses that produced them and to preceding actions. The episode-level baseline instead assigns one episode return to every action. On a fixed closed-loop protocol with real bioinformatics tools, ProtAgent-8B achieves 61.00% success under the annotation-coverage metric, compared with 41.60% for DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 671B and 60.80% for the strongest evaluated frontier system. In the three-seed comparison, mean success is 42.70% with episode-level returns and 61.40% with step-level returns under identity return normalization; the corresponding group-relative results are 36.50% and 58.20%. The metric measures recovery of reference annotations under this protocol; it does not by itself establish biological correctness or complete evidence grounding.

papers.title: MechGate: combining mechanism-derived measures of permeation and efflux to screen small molecule drugs targeting Escherichia coli
papers.summary: Most antibiotic molecules must cross the cell membrane and escape efflux pumps before hitting their targets. For de novo antibiotic design, very few of the in-silico-generated drug molecules can successfully pass these two steps. Existing evaluations of generated molecules do not separate these steps. Therefore, we introduce MechGate, a mechanism-resolved screening tool evaluating small drug molecules against E. coli, measuring permeation, efflux and antibacterial activity. After SMILES input, five measures are reported side by side: two for permeation via porins, one for permeation via the phospholipid membrane, one for efflux and one for activity. Each measure is read on its own, so a molecule that fails can be traced to the step that stops it. All features are taken from papers that state their mechanism rather than selected by importance ranking. On an external set of marketed antibacterials the measures give a precision of 0.789 to 0.873 against baselines near 0.44, and combining them the way the mechanism predicts raises precision to 0.92. We also find that the four public source libraries are separable from one another using physicochemical features alone; every measure here therefore draws both classes from a single library. All code is open-source and requires no commercial software.

papers.title: Sensorimotor behaviour from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
papers.summary: Connectomes now map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behaviour follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules join them: odours and looming objects drive sensory neurons, and motor neurons move the legs. Alone, the network passes a signal to the motor neurons it is known to drive when the pathway supplies about 2% or more of their input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to 95% of the odour sources. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches 18%, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none, so navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odour into avoidance, which requires the pairing and is odour-specific once one olfactory synapse class is scaled. An untrained connectome thus supports a behaviour and its learned reversal, and the pathways it cannot drive mark what the diagram leaves out.

papers.title: Benchmarking miRNA Target Prediction Methods
papers.summary: Background: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression by binding to target mRNAs. Although many tools predict miRNA-target interactions, predictions show limited concordance, and benchmarks relying on curated databases may be biased by overlap with tool-development data. Methods: We benchmarked seven tools (TargetScan, miRDB, miRmap, DIANA-microT, RNA22, miRWalk, and mirDIP) across approximately 59.7 million candidate miRNA-mRNA pairs. Each pair received an evidence-graded reference score (0-3) combining validated interactions from miRTarBase and TarBase with expression-derived evidence from paired miRNA-seq and mRNA-seq data in an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cohort of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and control lines. Performance was evaluated using Type I error, statistical power, and false discovery proportion (FDP). Robustness was assessed by increasing reference-score stringency (truth signal) and including progressively lower-confidence predictions (model signal). Optimal cutoffs maximized Youden's J statistic. Results: Rankings were largely consistent across settings. TargetScan and miRDB maintained Type I error rates below 0.05, with TargetScan showing the lowest FDP, but both had limited power. mirDIP achieved the highest power at the cost of the highest Type I error rate. At optimal cutoffs, mirDIP best balanced sensitivity and specificity (Youden's J = 0.566), followed by DIANA-microT (J = 0.481); miRWalk and RNA22 had FDPs near the random-prediction baseline. No tool was optimal across all metrics; tool and cutoff selection should reflect whether sensitivity or specificity is prioritized."""

papers.title: Tau creates spatially moving hotspots of amyloid-$\beta$ secondary nucleation: a reaction-diffusion model
papers.summary: Tau-amyloid-$\beta$ cross-seeding creates a spatial paradox. Bioavailable tau can promote A$\beta$42 nucleation, thereby increasing local fibril number and catalytic-site burden; yet the same fibrils consume the free A$\beta$ monomer required for homotypic secondary nucleation. The region containing the most tau or fibrillar material therefore need not be the region with the highest secondary-nucleation rate. We test this idea with a reaction-diffusion model that tracks a propagating effective tau catalyst, free A$\beta$ monomer, elongation-competent fibrils, fibril mass, and the catalytic sites exposed to monomer. The model reduces the spatial competition to two quantities: accessible catalytic sites and free monomer. Their balance yields an exact condition for an interior kinetic maximum: the logarithmic decrease in accessible catalytic sites must equal twice the logarithmic increase in free monomer. Two Damkohler numbers then separate the relevant competitions-elongation versus clearance, and elongation versus diffusive redistribution-while a monomer screening length sets the physical scale over which depletion can persist. Independent transport and turnover estimates place this length near 0.44-0.54 mm. Simulations show that tau first raises secondary nucleation near its source; continued fibril growth then produces a monomer-depleted wake, and the maximum shifts to a region with fewer catalytic sites but more available monomer. Oligomer transport and sustained reversible exchange can weaken or eliminate this contrast, whereas growth-history-dependent site density can strengthen it. The robust prediction is therefore a spatial separation among tau burden, fibril-mass growth, and instantaneous A$\beta$ secondary-nucleation activity, rather than a universal hotspot speed.

papers.title: New developments in the geometry and topology of 3D head-direction coding
papers.summary: The head-direction (HD) system is a neuronal compass that represents head orientation in 3D. Its encoding of 3D head orientation can be decomposed into a multiplexed representation of 2D head tilt relative to gravity and 1D head orientation in the horizontal plane (azimuth). Defining azimuth during 3D motion is not trivial, and recent studies have indicated that the HD system implements a so-called dual-axis/tilted-azimuth (DA/TA) rule, a representation that is well supported experimentally but remains mathematically and mechanistically difficult to interpret. Here, I introduce a new formulation of DA/TA based directly on the elements of a rotation matrix describing 3D head orientation. In this formulation, TA is represented by a 2D vector, whose direction encode TA and whose norm depends on tilt, consistent with a tilt-dependent gain of HD tuning reported by experimental studies. I provide a geometrical interpretation of this formulation and use it to characterize the topology of the resulting representation. More generally, I introduce a framework in which head orientation is represented by a rotation matrix and neuronal responses arise from linear combinations of its elements followed by nonlinear transformations. Within this framework, the linear stage specifies which aspects of 3D orientation are encoded, and therefore allow relating neuronal representation to linear algebra concepts. Classical HD tuning, gravity tuning, and DA/TA can all be described within this common framework. Together, these results provide a new mathematical, geometrical, and topological perspective on 3D HD coding.

papers.title: The dominance of feedback mechanisms for perception in the central visual field: the flip tilt illusion by backward masking and the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight algorithm
papers.summary: The flip tilt illusion is the misperception of the orientation of the alignment between a pair of dots by 90 degrees. It occurs when the dot-pair contains one black dot and one white dot, is typically visible only in the peripheral visual field. It is predicted by the central-peripheral dichotomy (CPD) theory. Along the visual pathway from retina to downstream stages, our brain admits only a tiny fraction of visual input information for recognition due to a processing bottleneck that starts from the output of the primary visual cortex (V1) along the visual pathway. Accordingly, perception downstream from V1 relies on impoverished information, selected largely by gaze shifts to center the selected content at fovea and additionally by the capacity of the bottleneck even in the central visual field, likely making perceptual hypotheses about the visual scene ambiguous or illusory. To overcome, downstream areas send feedback to upstream areas such as V1 to query for additional information, thereby re-assessing the weights of the initial hypotheses. This perceptual algorithm is termed Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW). To save resources, the feedback query is limited largely to the central visual field. The peripheral visual field is thus vulnerable to perceptual ambiguities and illusions. The CPD theory further predicts that impairing the feedback renders the flip tilt illusion visible in the central visual field. This paper reports a confirmation of the prediction. The feedback is disrupted by masking the visual inputs after a short viewing duration t. Furthermore, the FFVW algorithm is studied by a computational model of the perceptual data as a function of t. It reveals that the initial feedforward sweep of visual information explains the flip tilt illusion for t shorter than 20 ms, whereas the feedback mechanism dominates perception for longer t.

papers.title: Analysis of Biomarkers from Visual Explorations in Individuals Suspected to Be in the Prodromal Phase of Parkinson's Disease
papers.summary: Identifying prodromal Parkinson's Disease is a precondition for any future treatment that modifies the course of the disease, since such therapies would ideally act on the initial pathogenic events, early enough to delay the clinical onset of the disease rather than only slow its progression. In this work, a visual exploration model is retrained on an expanded corpus. Without any further training or threshold recalibration, it is then tested on an enriched cohort of patients with high risk of being in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's Disease, testing whether the learned signal follows a continuum of disease rather than only separating patients from controls. The resulting score distribution is analysed as an external evaluation of the hypothesis that the oculomotor signature targeted by the model is already partly present before clinical diagnosis. With every subject scored on data not used to train the model, the scores are ordered as controls < high-risk patients < Parkinson's Disease, with 42% of the high-risk patients exceeding the decision threshold. A SHAP decomposition of the scores into classifiers and gaze features shows that high scores in this cohort are driven mainly by reduced saccadic excursion, fewer fixations and longer fixations, the hypokinetic oculomotor profile that characterises Parkinson's Disease. The model score is also compared against the prodromal markers used for recruitment. The score is not correlated with hyposmia, constipation, depression or REM sleep behaviour disorder; these results, interpreted in the context of the selection induced by the recruitment criteria, are discussed as evidence that within the high-risk cohort the score is largely not explained by the available ancillary clinical variables. The results suggest that the visual biomarkers analysed are a complementary indicator to identify patients at risk of being in the prodromal stage.
